Part II EVOLUTION OF INDIAN FOREIGN POLICY

Chapter 4 The Foreign Policy of the Raj and Its Legacy Sneh Mahajan The ‘Raj or the ‘British Raj’ is the term usually used for the British Empire that extended over the Indian subcontinent from the mid-nineteenth century until 1947, and was com- monly called ‘India’ . The British had a clear concept of the region which they knew as ‘India’ and over which they established what became known as the British Empire in India, and which today forms India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. In the year 1600, the British established a chartered company to trade and called it the English East India Company. In 1773, when the British had established control only over the province of Bengal and small conclaves near Chennai and Mumbai, the Regulating Act was passed under which the Governor of Bengal was described as the ‘Governor General of British possessions in India’. The British took far-reaching precautions to prevent any European country from advancing towards India. In 1798, when Napoleon invaded Egypt, the British government thought in terms of organizing a distance defense for the entire region that lay on the route to India. In July 1807, when Napoleon and Tsar Alexander I held discussions about a joint invasion of India and signed the Treaty of Tilsit, it asked the Government of India to send friendly missions to all states that lay between India and Europe—Punjab, Sind, Muscat, Afghanistan, and Persia. By 1856, the British had brought India under either their direct rule or indirect control through what they described as ‘the Indian Princes’ . The British Empire in India was too massive ever to fall under the aegis of the Colonial Office. It was governed as a distinct unit. London needed a strong central government in India, obedient to it, yet capable of keeping the provincial administrations in line with metropolitan purposes. Step by step, the British built their Empire on the administrative structure that existed under the Mughals from the center to the tehesil level. In the nineteenth century, when the British established their control over India, Britain was the ‘top’ nation. The British policy-makers wanted to maintain Britain’s standing as a great power. It is generally held that Britain’s great power status was based

52 Sneh Mahajan on three things—its industrial and commercial strength, its naval supremacy, and its worldwide empire. However, trade and the navy were merely instruments of power. It was Britain’s Empire that was the most visible expression of Britain’s standing in the affairs of the world. The Indian Empire formed 97 per cent of Britain’s Asiatic Empire. In Britain’s worldwide Empire, in terms of population, in 1912, of every 100 persons in Britain and its Empire (dependent and self-governing together), ten lived in the United Kingdom, five lived in self-governing dominions, 12 in all other colonies put together, and 73 lived in the Indian Empire alone (Davis and Huttonback 1986: 28). The Indian Empire, with its immense human and material resources, its huge army, and its great importance to the British economy, always featured high in the calcula - tions of the British. There is compelling evidence to show that, in Britain as well as in all European countries, it was taken for granted that loss of India would be a great blow to Britain. India’s substantial contribution to the two World Wars reiterated emphati- cally that India was an imperial asset. The First World War galvanized nationalist senti- ment in India. The British government passed Government of India Acts in 1919 and 1935 ostensibly for ‘the gradual development of self-governing institutions’ . However, now historians accept that the aim of the government was not to prepare Indians for self-government but to prolong their rule by winning over the support of a section of Indian leaders. Britain’s determination to retain hold over India did not falter until after the end of the Second World War. The most important feature of the Government of India’s foreign policy until 1947 was that, being a colony of the British, its foreign policy was decided in the interest of the British. A colony or a colonial state is a regime through which a colonial power, i.e. an external entity, governs with a view to deriving maximum benefit from the resources and labor within that colony. The grand strategy adopted by the British aimed at ensuring full security to the Indian Empire, protecting all routes between Britain and India, and ensuring that India’s trade and commerce were carried on in Britain’s inter- est. Generations of historians have argued that the strategic and political needs of the British were different from, and occasionally in conflict with, those of India and that the Government of India enjoyed considerable liberty of action especially in determin- ing relations with other states in Asia. Four types of explanations are advanced in this connection. First, the distance between Britain and India enabled the Government of India to act in its own way either by calculated design or inadvertently. Second, ‘the man on the spot’ tended to act in such ways as not to leave much choice to the authorities at London. Third, it is argued that the execution of policies in any case lay with the gov - ernment at Kolkata/New Delhi, and, finally, that the Government of India maintained direct relations with the states in the neighborhood. But, as already said, British India’s foreign policy was decided at London and wholly in Britain’s interest. This created essential unity of purpose and harmony between the authorities in London and Kolkata/New Delhi.1 The Foreign Office, the War Office, the India Office and the Government of India all became associated with the external relations and the security of the Indian Empire, sifted and exchanged information regarding the motives and military potentialities of states in the vicinity of India, and coordinated different

The Foreign Policy of the Raj and Its Legacy 53 plans of action. But, in the end, it was the decision of the government at London that pre- vailed. The mere hierarchy of power ensured that. The Government of India remained an arm of the government at London. Foreign policy of the Government of British India was the foreign policy of the British, for the British, and by the British. Guarding the Land Frontier The land frontier of Britain’s Indian Empire extended in a half circle touching from west to east –Iran, Afghanistan, Tibet, Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan, and Burma. The Government of India was entrusted with the task of handling relations with all these states (except Iran). The British did not apprehend danger to their Indian Empire from any of these. Inside India, there were French conclaves at Pondicherry, and Portuguese in Goa, Daman, and Diu. But given Britain’s naval superiority, these did not cause anxiety. The British rulers of India constantly adopted a policy of interposing a protected state between the actual possessions they administered and the possessions of formidable neighbors whom they desired to keep at arm’s length. This state in between was called the ‘buffer’ state. In fact, the buffer state as a concept of international politics is primarily of British-Indian coinage and came into vogue somewhere in the 1880s. The buffer state was given internal freedom, but was expected to exclude all extraneous influences in the conduct of foreign relations. It thus accepted derogation of sovereignty. It was not even a satellite state. A buffer state would break down if any attempt was made to convert it into a satellite (Mehra 2007: 114–15). In 1902, Lord Lansdowne, the Foreign Secretary, who had been the Viceroy of India (1884–94) and later, the Secretary for War, defined a buffer zone as ‘an intervening zone sufficient to prevent direct contact between the dominions of Great Britain and those of other great military Powers’ .2 In the nineteenth century, the British gradually built up a series of buffers along the landward periphery of the Indian Empire. In the parlance of the Raj this system became known as ‘the ring fence’ . They maintained Iran, Afghanistan, and Tibet as the outer ring. The three Himalayan states—Nepal, Bhutan, and Sikkim—were maintained as the inner ring. These formed a territorial buffer between India, and China and Tibet. These states in the vicinity of India remained weak and economically ‘undeveloped’ . The British did not apprehend danger to their Indian Empire from any of these. Beyond these states lay the Russian Empire and the Chinese Empire. Relations with Russia and China were maintained by the British government at London. The foreign policy of British India was determined at London though there were constant consultations between the gov- ernments of Britain and India. From the 1860s, the security policy in India centered on defense against the expan - sion of the Tsarist Empire towards the northwest frontier. In the direction of Kabul, it occupied Tashkent in 1865, Bukhara in 1866, and Samarkand in 1868. Babar had invaded India in the 1520s from Samarkand. The occupation of Merv in 1884 brought the Russian Empire almost to the Afghan frontier. In the 1890s, the British government tried to settle

54 Sneh Mahajan the issue by demarcating the frontier of Afghanistan—between the Indian Empire and Afghanistan in 1893 and the Russian Empire and Afghanistan in 1895. These were not drawn on an ethnic, cultural, or economic basis. The sole aim was to avoid having a frontier contiguous to the Russia Empire. In Afghanistan, a long corridor which became known as the Wakhan Corridor—220 kilometers in length and 16–60 kilometers in width—was created. The problem became worse confounded when, towards the end of the nineteenth century, Russia started building railways in Central Asia. After the Franco- Russian Alliance of 1894, France began to provide funds for building these rail- ways. With this it seemed that Russia was overcoming the biggest obstacle—distance. Moreover, in case of Russia’s invasion of India, the French navy could delay the sending of British troops to India. The fear generated by Russia’s expansion became known as ‘Russophobia’ . Why did the expansion of Russia cause such anxiety at London? The reason was that the British knew that the Raj was based on the awe of British arms and not on the con- sent of Indians. Any defeat by the Russian army, even on the remote frontier in a mere skirmish, could create a spasm of sedition from one end of India to another. Besides, by taking advantage of Britain’s vulnerability on the Indian frontier, Russia could extract concessions from Britain elsewhere. The British navy could not move on wheels. From the beginning of the nineteenth century, Britain’s strategic preoccupation with this threat to the Indian Empire became a major component of Britain’s foreign policy in general and defense of the Indian Empire in particular (Mahajan 2002: chs. 1 and 4). In this background, in 1902, the British government appointed the Committee of Imperial Defence to advise on the grand strategy to be adopted for the defense of Empire. It became the direct link between military experts and the Cabinet and had the potential to influence foreign as well as defense policy. The Government of India was kept well-informed. Since its inception in 1902, the War Office and the India Office agreed that, in view of the construction of railways in Central Asia by Russia, it was diffi- cult to defend India from Russian assault as the British did not have adequate manpower and the material resources to defend India from a position of strength. Such was the determination to hold on to India that grotesque plans like keeping some army units in South Africa to reinforce the Indian army and requisitioning soldiers from Japan were discussed.3 The issue of lack of means to defend the Indian Empire was one of the rea- sons for opting for a diplomatic solution—the signing of the Anglo-Russian Convention in 1907. During the First World War, Britain, France, and Russia joined the war against Germany on the same side. Even after the collapse of the Tsarist Empire in 1917, the War Office remained con - vinced that Soviet Russia would strike a blow at the Indian Empire as soon as its forces were ready. The threat was exacerbated by the Bolshevik ideology that projected itself as the enemy of imperialism. Down to 1940 when Russia joined the Second World War on the side of Britain, the problem of defense of India against Russia’s designs remained the central preoccupation of British foreign and defense policies. PARDESI This paper will provide a survey of India’s foreign policy from 1947 to the present day. It is divided into three distinct historical sections. It will also attempt to explain the underlying reasons for these policies, India’s initial orientation, and su bsequent shifts that occurred over time. The first section deals with the period from 1947 to 1962, the second from 1962 to 1991 and the third from 1991 to the present. The choice of these three segments is far from arbitrary. The first period constituted the most idealistic pha se of India’s foreign policy under the tutelage of India’s first Prim e Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. The second began with India’s disastrous defeat in the 1962 Sino-Indian border war. This period saw a gradual shift away from the early idealism that had characterized the country’s foreign policy and the adoption of an increasingly “self-help” approach to foreign policy while retaining elements of the Nehruvian rhetoric. 1 The third phase began with the end of the Cold War and the adoption of a more pragmatic foreign policy hewing closely to the principles of Realism.2 The Sources of India’s Foreign Policy Systemic, national and decision-mak ing factors helped shape post- independence India’s foreign policy choices.3 However, this paper will argue that India’s poli cymakers chose, quite deliberately, to ignore systemic constraints and decided to pursue an explicitly ideational foreign policy and with mostly disastrous consequences.4 The pursuit of such a policy left India utterly u nprepared to cope with a serious security threat from the People’s Republic of China and culminated in a disastrous border war in 1962. text: Explaining Sixty Years of India’s Foreign Policy 5 war did India embark on a “self-help” strategy designed to guarantee its security.5 The systemic constraints on India’s foreign policy stemmed from the onset of the Cold War which virtually coincided with India’s independence in 1947. Interestingly enough, neither the Soviet Union nor the United States evinced any great interest in India at the onset of the Cold War. The United States was virtually ignorant about India and had few cultural, strategic or economic links with the nascent nation.6 Consequently, in the immediate aftermath of India’s indepen- dence it paid scant attention to India. Simultaneously, the Soviet Union did not attach any strategic significance to India. 7 This mutual lack of interest in India actually worked to India’s advantage as it gave the country considerable room for maneuver. However, at a regional level, the dis- tribution of power placed India at a disadvantage. The other major regional state, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) posed a significant security threat to India, one which it chose to ignore at its peril.8 At a national level, the memories of colonial rule contributed to a political culture which privileged the concept of national autonomy. The desire to maintain the greatest possible independence in the conduct of India’s foreign affairs was a se ntiment that pervaded the country. Public opinion, to the limited extent that it was concerned with foreign affairs, would find any notion of de ference to external powers to be intolerable.9 The country had been under the yoke of colonial rule for 200 years and the weight of this colonial past was considerable. Not surprisingly, India’s post- independence policymakers were acutely sensitive to the significance of this colonial legacy. Accord- ingly, they explicitly sought to forge a pathway that would keep India outside the ambit of the Cold War. Such a strategy was possible because anti-imperialist sentiments were widespread within the Indian polity across the political spectrum. 10 This strategy came to be known as nonalignment and Indian policymakers were at pains to distinguish it from “neutralism.”11 The real architect of this policy was Prime Minister Nehru. Even though he was temperamentally a Western liberal, he was deeply skeptical of the United States. 12 In part, his skepti cism was the conse- quence of his highly Anglicized personal and professional background. In effect, he had come to share the British upper class disdain for the United States. His views toward the Soviet Union were more ambivalent. He was cognizant of the horrors of Stalin’s collectivist enterprise

text: 6 India Review though admiring of the achievements of the forced-draught industrial- ization program. His partiality to ward the USSR also stemmed from his own social democratic predilections. At least two factors can be adduced to explain Nehru’s adoption of nonalignment as the lodestar of In dia’s foreign policy. First, he was acutely concerned about the opportunity costs of defense spending. Any involvement with the two emerging blocs, he feared, would draw India into the titanic struggle and divert critical resources from economic development. 13 Second, he was intent on maintaining India’s hard-won independence. Moving into the ambit of either superpower could com- promise such freedom of maneuver. The Pathway to 1962 From the time of independence to th e disastrous border conflict with the PRC, three key features characterized India’s foreign policy. First, India played a significant role in multilateral institutions and particularly in United Nations peacekeeping operations. Second, it also emerged as a critical proponent of the nonaligned movement. Third, as a leader of the nonaligned movement it also made a significant contribution toward the process of decolonization. These three critical commitments, in turn, manifested themselves at global, regional and national levels. At a global level, India attempted to defuse Cold War tensions in a number of contexts, regional and functional. To that end, India had emerged as one of the early propo- nents of a nuclear test ban treaty and in 1952 had introduced a draft resolution co-sponsored with Irela nd to bring about a global ban on nuclear tests. In the event, thanks to the exigencies of Cold War politics, little or nothing came of this effo rt. Nevertheless, this endeavor was a manifestation of India’s interest in forging a particular global order, one which would hobble the use of force in international affairs. India also sought to play a vital role in United Nations peacekeeping opera- tions as well as the peaceful resolution of regional disputes. In pursuit of these ends India became involv ed in the International Control Commission in Vietnam along with Canada and Poland, it was a key member of the Neutral Nations Re patriation Commission in Korea and it also made a significant troop contribution to the United Nations Peacekeeping forces in the Belgian Congo. 14 Additionally, India proved to be a tireless campaigner in the effort to bring about decolonization. To that end, India’s diplomacy was carefully geared to the discussion

text: Explaining Sixty Years of India’s Foreign Policy 7 of the issue at various internationa l fora and especially in the Non- Aligned Movement (NAM). In the region, it refe rred the Kashmir dispute with Pakistan to the United Nations for possible resoluti on. To the dismay of its policy- makers, the issue became quickly embroiled in the politics of the Cold War.15 As a consequence of the largely partisan discussions at the United Nations, India’s political leadership became increasingly disil- lusioned about the resolution of its bilateral territorial disputes through the mechanism of the United Nations. Not surprisingly, after extensive diplomatic discussion with the intransigent Salazar regime in Portugal produced a deadlock and Prime Minister Nehru faced increasing criticism from a group of Afro-Asian leaders, India chose to use force to oust the Portuguese from their colonial enclave in Goa in 1960. 16 Finally, at national level, the country’s commitment to nonalignment led to the adoption of a particular set of significant policy choices. Specifically, one of the key elements of the doctrine of nonalignment was the limitation of high defense expenditures. 17 To this end India pursued the policy of Panchsheel (o r the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence) towards the PRC. The five principles were mutual respect for each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty; non-aggression; non-interference in one another’s internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; and peaceful coexistence. 18 As a consequence, Indian military expenditures were drastically lim ited even when steady evidence about a possible security threat from the PRC continued to mount. 19 Such a policy, unfortunately, proved to be extremely costly when the border negotiations with the PRC ultimately reached a cul-de-sac in 1960. Faced with this situation, India embarked upon a strategy of compellence designed to restore what it deemed to be the territorial status quo along the disputed Himalayan border. 20 This policy, how- ever, was singularly ill conceived as it involved sending in lightly armed, poorly equipped and ill-pre pared troops to high altitudes in “penny packets.” In October 1962, when the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) attacked with considerable force, the Indian military was grossly unprepared to face the onslaught. The PLA inflicted consider- able losses on the Indian forces and then withdrew from some of the areas that they had entered. However, they did not vacate some 14,000 square miles that they had initially claimed. 21 These territories and some other disputed regions still remain the subject of tortured and glacial border negotiations.22

text: 8 India Review “Modified Structuralism”: The Post-Nehru Era23 The military defeat in 1962 marked nothing short of a watershed in the structure and conduct of India’ s foreign and security policies. In the immediate aftermath of this military debacle Nehru overcame his staunch objections to defense spending. In his final days, he oversaw a drastic re-appraisal of India’s security policies and practices. Most importantly, India embarked on a substantial program of military modernization. It committed itself to the creation of a million-strong army with ten new mountain divisi ons equipped and trained for high altitude warfare, a 45-squadron air force with supersonic aircraft and a modest program of naval expansion. 24 However, even after Nehru’s demise in 1964, his successors sti ll could not formally abandon the stated adherence to a policy of nonalignment. Consequently, the rhet- oric of nonalignment remained a st aple of Indian foreign policy. India’s foreign policy behavior, however, increasingly assumed a more Realist orientation. Once again, global, regional, and personal factors contributed to the major policy shift. Despite a fleetin g moment of military cooperation with India in the aftermath of the 1962 war, the United States disen- gaged itself from South Asia afte r the second Indo-Pakistani conflict in 1965 as it became increasingly preoccupied with the prosecution of the Vietnam War. 25 Barring a brief and unhappy interlude in 1966 when the Johnson administration chose to exert considerable economic pressure on India to temper its criticism of the Vietnam War, to reform its agricultural policies and to open up its domestic economy to foreign investment, the United States, for all practical purposes, lost interest in India.26 Sensing an opportunity to expand their influence in the subcontinent, the Soviets brokered a peace agreement between India and Pakistan in the Central Asian city of Tashkent in 1966. With this American disen- gagement from the subcontinent, Pakistan sought to expand the scope of its security cooperation with the PRC to balance Indian power, thereby contributing to a growing security nexus between India’s two major adversaries. At a regional level, India’s misgiv ings about its security increased in the aftermath of the first Chinese nuclear test at Lop Nor in 1964.27 The political fallout from these te sts was considerable. Some within India’s parliament called for an abandonment of nonalignment and even urged that India acquire an independent nuclear weapons option.

text: Explaining Sixty Years of India’s Foreign Policy 9 After considerable debate, the ru ling Congress party and the new Prime Minister, Lal Bahadur Shastri, reaffirmed the country’s public commitment to nonalignment and eschewed any immediate plans to acquire nuclear weapons. However, in 1966, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, Shastri’s successor, decided to seek a nuclear guarantee from the great powers. This effort proved to be quite fruitless. 28 In the aftermath of this failure, Prime Minister Gandhi authorized India’s Subterranean Nuclear Explosions Project (SNEP) which culminated in India’s first nuclear test of May 1974.29 Under Indira Gandhi, India’s foreign policy sought to sustain two competing visions of world order. On the one hand, India still supported the cause of decolonization and continued to lead the charge on behalf of the weaker states in the international system. For example, it remained a staunch opponent of the apartheid regime in South Africa, it was an unyieldi ng supporter of the Palestinian cause and it opposed the Portuguese colonial presence in Angola and Mozambique. On the other hand, it also came to accept the importance of defense preparedness and increasingly overcame its reservations about the use of force in international politics. Not surprisingly, when faced with several million refu gees from East Pakistan as a consequence of the outbreak of a civil war, the country quickly forged a careful politico- diplomatic strategy to break up Pakistan. 30 Part of this strategy involved the acquisition of a tacit security guarantee from the Soviet Union to counter possible Chinese malfeasan ce. Accordingly, despite India’s professed commitment to nonalignment it signed a 20-year pact of “peace, friendship and cooperation” with the Soviet Union in August 1971. With its northern flanks thereby protected, India had a free hand to intervene in East Pakistan. Fortunately, Pakistan’s attack on its northern air bases in early December gave it the casus belli to launch an attack on the eastern front. Wi thin two weeks, the Indian army along with an indigenous Bengali rebel movement, the “mukti bahini” (literally “liberation force”), mili tarily prevailed against the demoral- ized Pakistani forces.31 In the aftermath of the 1971 wa r, the concomitant break-up of Pakistan and the creation of Bangladesh, India emerged as the undis- puted dominant power within the subcontinent. Despite its new-found status, the country was unable to transcend the region. Several factors account for this failure to emerge as a power

Most importantly, thanks to its pursuit of a dubious strategy of state-led industrialization India’s economic growth remained anemic. 32 Simultaneously, the country’s deep-seated export pessimism led it to shy away from integrating itself into the global economy. The failure to develop ties with the global economy contributed to a paucity of foreign investment, important technological lags, a lack of innova tion, and the stifling of entrepre- neurship. In turn, these forces contributed to what the eminent Indian economist Raj Krishna mordantly referred to as the “Hindu rate of growth.” 33 India’s political choices at systemic and national levels also did very little to enhance it global stature. At a global level, in the wake of the first oil crisis of 1973, India chose to spearhead the Group of 77, a set of developing nations seeking to fundamentally alter the global economic order. Ironically, while it was a leader of this coalition it benefited little from the global spike in oil prices and failed to obtain any meaningful concessions as a resource-poor developing nation from the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). Indeed the country’s economic weakness effectively prevented it from carrying through a viable nuclear weapons program even after it managed to successfully test a nuclear weapon in May 1974. Faced with widespread global diplomatic disapprobation and significant economic and technological sanctions, India’s policymakers chose not carry out any further tests.34 Enter the Bear Throughout much of the decade of the 1970s, thanks to its poor record of economic growth and its diplomatic limitations, India became a marginal player in the global order. Its influence remained confined to the South Asian region. Its insignificance was again underscored when the Soviets invaded Afghanistan in December 1979.35 The United States paid scant attention to Indian sensibilities and concerns when it chose to forge a renewed strategic relation ship with Pakistan almost imme- diately after the Soviet invasion. General Zia-ul-Haq even rebuffed India’s efforts at reassuring Pakistan in the aftermath of the invasion.36 In its efforts to oust the Soviets from Afghanistan the United States came to rely heavily on Pakistan. (The second package was not fully delivered because the So viets withdrew from Afghanistan in 1990 and the United States al so imposed economic sanctions on Pakistan for its pursuit of a clandestine nuclear weapons program. 37) In an effort to maintain its milit ary superiority over Pakistan, India entered into a tighter military cooperation relationship with the Soviet Union. This military relationship, however, exacted a significant diplo- matic cost. India was forced to taci tly acquiesce in the Soviet occupa- tion of Afghanistan. 38 For the remainder of the decade, barring some limited efforts on the part of the Reagan administration to improve relations with India as part of a strategy to reduce the country’s dependence on the Soviet Union, India remained of little consequence to the great powers.39 A Requiem for Nonalignment? Few events, barring the shock of the 1962 Sino-Indian border war, has had as much of an impact on India’ s foreign and security policies as the collapse of the Soviet Union and the concomitant end of the Cold War. The Soviet collapse and the transformation of the global order forced India’s policymakers to make drastic changes in India’s foreign policy at multiple levels. At a global level, nonalignment ceased to have much meaning. As a former Indian foreign, and subsequently prime minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, quite succinctly stated, “It is a mantra that we have to keep repeating, but who are you going to be nonaligned against?” With the end of nonalignment for all practical purposes, India’s foreign policy was suddenly bereft of a grand strate- gic vision. At another level, the country was also confronted with an unprece- dented fiscal crisis partly as a consequence of the first Gulf War of 1991. Three factors contributed to this crisis. First, anticipating a spike in oil prices because of Saddam Hu ssein’s invasion and occupation of Kuwait, India had purchased considerable amounts of petroleum on the spot market thereby draining it s treasury of much-needed foreign exchange. Second, the government of India was forced to repatriate over 100,000 workers from the Persian Gulf at short notice. Third, it lost the very substant ial remittances that the workers from the Gulf had contributed to the Indian exch equer. The confluence of these three factors placed the country in dire financial straits. 40 Faced with

text: 12 India Review this extraordinary crisis and also confronting the loss of the vast East European market as a consequence of the Soviet collapse, India’s policymakers, most notably the then Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, chose to dramatically alter India’s domestic and international economic policies.41 These involved abandoning the country’s historic commitment to import-substituting industrialization, unbundling, though fitfully at best, its vast public sector and dismantling a labyrin- thine set of regulations, licenses, permits and quotas which had largely stifled economic growth.42 While the crisis itself was the precipitating cause of India’s economic reform s, the exogenous shock was not a sufficient condition. The piecemeal reforms of the 1980s under Prime Ministers Indira Gandhi and Raji v Gandhi had generated consensus about the desirability of economic li beralization at least a year prior to the balance-of-payments crisis.43 Finding opportunity in the crisis, the Indian executive proceeded with reforms as it was convinced that global economic integration was im perative for India for factors beyond the immediate crisis.44 Drastic changes were also undertaken in the political arena. As argued earlier, India’s commitme nt to nonalignment had already eroded in practice, if not in rhetoric, in the post-Nehru era. Now its policymakers sought to forge a new vision for the country. However, the country lacked a leader of the stature and intellec tual proclivities of Jawaharlal Nehru. Yet the Prime Minister, Narasimha Rao, possessed a sufficient grasp of international a ffairs to recognize the necessity of charting a new course for the country in both domestic and interna- tional arenas. 45 Accordingly, he sought to chart a new course for the country’s foreign policy. This effort to alter the country’s foreign policy orientation toward the emergent, sole superpower, the United States, ran into important hurdles for three compelling reasons. First, at a global level the United States had few significant interests in India barring nonproliferation. This issue put the two sides on a collision course as India was a staunch opponent of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT) and categor- ically refused to accede to its exp ectations. The US, especially, under the Clinton administration, was committed to its indefinite and uncondi- tional extension at the Review Conference in 1995. Not surprisingly, their fundamental differences put the two countries at odds. Second, at a regional level, even though the US Department of Com- merce under the stewardship of Secretary of Commerce, Ron Brown,

text: Explaining Sixty Years of India’s Foreign Policy 13 had anointed India as one of the world’s “big emer ging markets,” American investment in and trade with India was so negligible that the nonproliferation issue overshadowed other interests. Third and finally, at a bureaucrat ic level in both countries the “shadow of the past” weighed heavily on all deliberations. Most Indian foreign policy bureaucrats were dubious about American goals and interests in South Asia and there was lingering distrust of India in both the State and Defense departme nts in the United States. These mutual misgivings hobbled the growth of the relationship even though some small progress had been made in the last days of Indira Gandhi, and her son and successor, Rajiv Gandhi. As a consequence of these three factors, improvements in relations were, at best fitful, and frequently hostage to minor, episodic differences. For example, the Assistant Secretary of State Robin Raphael’s careless remark about Kashmir’s accession to India at a press briefing in Washington, DC became a major diplomatic contretemps. 46 However, Indian policymakers ma naged to move with somewhat greater dexterity on other fronts. To that end, they ended the country’s reflexive support for th e Arab position on Israel and the Palestinian question. Historically, since the creation of the state of Israel in 1948, for reasons of both domestic politics and national ideol- ogy, India had adopted a mostly frosty approach toward the Jewish state. At home Indian policymakers were attentive to the sentiments of the Muslim population. At an ideological level they had viewed the creation of Israel as the continuation of a colonial policy. 47 In 1992, in the wake of the Oslo Accord between Israel and the Palestinians, India upgraded its diplomatic relations with Israel to the ambassado- rial level. Simultaneously, India also directed its gaze toward Southeast Asia after a long span of neglect. During much of the Cold War Indian pol- icymakers had shunned the states of Southeast Asia, with the critical exception of Vietnam, viewing th em as mostly American puppets. Now, as part and parcel of the opening of its markets to foreign investment and seeking to develop a viable export sector, the country embarked upon a “Look East policy.” 48 While it is commonly believed that the underlying rationale behind India’s engagement with Southeast Asia has been India’s domestic economic liberalization, it must be noted that India had begun to seek purposeful politico-military engagement with Southeast Asia almost simultaneously. text: 14 India Review strategic engagement of Southeast Asian reflected in its “Look East” policy stemmed from India’s search for new friends and partners after the loss of its superpower patron in 1991. At the same time, India was determined to break out of the South Asian strategic box that it had found itself confined to after its defeat in the 1962 Sino-Indian border war. India began to engage Southeast Asia in search of a larger role in Asia and to prevent that region from being dominated by Chinese economic and military power. 49 Closer to home, the Narasimha Rao regime’s efforts continued to improve relations with the PRC, a process that had been initiated dur- ing the Rajiv Gandhi regime in the late 1980s. Even though the two sides forged two important confidence-b uilding measures (CBMs) in 1993 and 1996 designed to reduce tensions along the Line of Actual Control, little or no progress was made in resolving the border dispute.50 Finally, relations with Pakistan , India’s long-st anding adversary remained contentious as ever. In considerable part the relationship with Pakistan deteriorated because of the outbreak of an ethno-religious insurgency in the disputed state of Jammu and Kashmir in December 1989. The origins of this insurgen cy were mostly indigenous and could be traced to a process of growing political mobilization against a backdrop of steady institutional decay.51 However, with the outbreak of the insurgency Pakistan’s policymakers quickly stepped into the fray and helped transform a largely internal uprising into an ideologi- cally charged, sanguinary, extortion racket. 52 In an attempt to suppress the insurgency India resorted to a time- honored counterinsurgency strategy. This involved the substantial use of force against the insurgents but with the promise of free and fair elections once they proved willing to abandon their secessionist agenda. As with other counterinsurgency op erations, this strategy has met with some success. Ho wever, while it has reduced the insurgency to manageable proportions, it has not been able to eliminate it altogether. Continued Pakistani logistical support for the insurgents, the provision of sanctuaries in Pakistan-controlled Kashmir and a porous border has prevented India from successfully suppressing the insurgency. Crossing the Nuclear Rubicon and Beyond Pakistan’s needling of India in Kashmir was and remains susceptible to management through India’s conventional military capabilities.53 Nor do Pakistan’s conventional capabilities pose an especially compelling

text: Explaining Sixty Years of India’s Foreign Policy 15 threat to India’s security.54 The conventional military capabilities, the persistence of the border disput e and the PRC’s nuclear weapons posed an altogether different orde r of threat to India’s security. Indeed it was the long-term securi ty threats that the PRC posed to India that proved to be the most compelling underlying factor that drove India’s nuclear weapons program. 55 The specific timing of the program, contrary to much polemical writing on the subject had little to do with the ascendance of the right-of-center Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to power. 56 Instead it was closely tied to the successful extension of the NPT in 1995 and the seeming inexorable efforts of the Clinton administration to conc lude a comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty. Fearful that the passage of the test ban treaty was all but inevitable, Indian policymakers chose to exercise the nuclear option before ineluctable pressures were br ought to bear on India to accede to the regime. Despite the initial burst of hostility from the United States and the other great powers, the internati onal community has come to grudg- ingly accept India as a de facto nuclear weapons state. In large part this came about as a consequence of extended bilate ral negotiations between US Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and Jaswant Singh, the Indian Minister for External Affairs. 57 Indeed, it is possible to argue that these talks helped provide a foundation for the Bush administration’s subsequent attempts to woo India. One of the most significant steps that the Bush administration took in its attempt to cement the relationship was the offe r of a substantial civilian nuclear deal which holds the promise of ending India’s nuclear isolation. 58 Even though the deal remains in abeyance, the Indo-US relationship is now on a far more secure footing than during the past several decades. The alarmist claims of a host of scholars and policymakers about a possible nuclear exchange between India and Pakistan have not mate- rialized. Pakistan’s feckless attempt to revive the Kashmir issue through its incursion in the Kargil region did contribute to a limited war between the two states in 1999. 59 However, despite the Pakistani provocation India exercised remarkable restrain t and a large-scale war was effec- tively avoided. Similarly, in the aftermath of the terrorist attack on the Indian parliament in December 2001 India resorted to a strategy of coercive diplomacy albe it with mixed results. 60 It is important to underscore that neither of these two crises culminated in a full-scale war between the two long-standing adversaries. text: 16 India Review the 2001–2002 crisis, India and Pakistan, with some American prodding, embarked upon a peace process. The results from this process have been limited though it has resulted in some de-escalation of tensions on the Kashmir front.61 India Resurgent? Where is India’s foreign policy h eaded in the post-Cold War era? Obviously the structure of the in ternational system has changed beyond recognition since the immedi ate post-war era. Consequently, India’s room for maneuver has chan ged dramatically and to a large extent India’s policymakers have responded with some dexterity to those changes in the global order. Their responses, at economic, politi- cal and strategic levels have enabled India to emerge as a potential great power though it still faces enormous developmental challenges.62 These challenges include sustaining th e country’s economic growth rate, ensuring energy security, and resolving the country’s internal security problems within the framework of its democratic and secular institu- tions. At the same time, India must work with its fragile neighbors to ensure that they flou rish politically, economically, and even ecologi- cally. New Delhi needs to proactively shape its regional environment in tandem with its neighbors. Though numerous and formidable, these challenges are not beyond the reach of India’s policy establishment. India needs a clear vision, the requis ite political and institutional will, and effective leadership to address these challenges. In particular, there are three important strategic questions confronting the Indian leader- ship. First, how do they manage the contentious relationship with Pakistan even if they cannot br ing about a rapprochement on the Kashmir question? Second, how does India respond to and cope with the extraordinary rise of the PRC? Third and finally, what sort of rela- tionship will India forge with the United States in the ensuing decades? There are no clear-cut answers to these questions. However, much of the future direction and substa nce of India’s foreign policy will necessarily revolve around those subjects. NOTES 1. text: From non-alignment to multi-alignment: assessing India’s foreign policy shift Rahul Mishra Centre for ASEAN Regionalism Universiti Malaya (CARUM), Asia-Europe Institute, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia ABSTRACT Establishing a non-aligned bloc at the height of the power politics- ridden Cold War era was one of the most profound normative contributions India made to the modern international order. This article argues that NAM was a pragmatic yet principled approach to dealing with a world dominated by divisive power politics. For India, non-alignment still lives on to a certain extent in the form of its spirited defence of strategic autonomy and the recent itera - tion of ‘multi-alignment’ in Indian foreign policy to deal with an uncertain world. KEYWORDS Cold War; India; Jawaharlal Nehru; Multi-alignment; Non–Aligned Movement (NAM); strategic autonomy; world order Introduction The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) played two critical roles in shaping the post-Second World War world order. First, it aided in stabilising the bipolar world dynamics, which were prone to conflict. Second, it provided post-colonial states with a common platform to raise their interests and concerns in shaping the international order. NAM was instrumental in proposing new set of normative ideas to the international system, some of which were inducted into the system eventually. Regional organisations such as ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) took inspiration from NAM in ways more than one. The role played by India in shaping NAM – and by extension in influencing the international order – is still underappreciated, particularly among the western international relations theorists. At the height of the Cold War, when India was grappling with an excessively polarised international system, NAM turned out to be an effective and rather powerful diplomatic tool in ensuring India’s strategic autonomy in the international arena. For the most part, it contributed to strengthening the cherished principles of keeping foreign policy inde - pendent and even-handed. India contributed to NAM in creating its normative agency, which was established as a forum comprising countries from Africa and Asia that believed in discarding ideological-material rivalries among states and in pursuing their own paths to growth and development. In the early post-World War II era, newly- independent states such as India Egypt, Indonesia, and Yugoslavia possessed diplomatic capacities that allowed them to swing international opinion away from either of the two power blocs. Their assistance was pivotal in shaping international opinions on key issues. text: In most cases, the support of the non-aligned bloc was not only crucial but was also seen as a voice of reason, which is why both the US-led Western bloc and the USSR-led Socialist bloc tried to woo the NAM countries. Such has been the impact of those early successes in India’s foreign policy that even today – when India has drawn closer than ever to the US and is a part of the Quad (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue) multi-aligned and principled inclusivity continue to prevail as a foreign policy priority. In recent years, Indian Minister of External Affairs S. Jaishankar and foreign secretary Harsh Vardhan Shringla have repeatedly underscored the critical role strategic autonomy plays in shaping Indian foreign policy choices. S. Jaishankar, the External Affairs Minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet (2019–2024), has described it as India’s pursuit of multi-alignment (Jaishankar, 2020 ). In his recent speech at the Raisina Dialogue, in 2022, Dr. Jaishankar also acknowledged that the term ‘multi-alignment’ was first floated by Shashi Tharoor, an Indian politician (Tharoor, 2022 ). India’s non-aligned foreign policy: origin and evolution A newly independent India’s foreign and security policies and practices were heavily influenced by its more-than-a-century-old struggle for independence. During the free - dom struggle, Indian freedom fighters realised that India was not alone in its freedom struggle; there were dozens of countries in the non-western world fighting against the exploitation at the hands of the Western Imperialist powers. Years of violent and non-violent struggles and systemic factors of global politics had a considerable impact on these countries. Consequently, a majority of these countries perceived their independence as the ‘dawn of a new era’ – an era beyond the ‘dark ages’ where nations, particularly the newly independent ones, must live in peace and harmony. True, some countries had teething troubles in their nation-building and ethnic reconci - liation processes or even had boundary disputes with neighbours; but, none of these challenges were as daunting as the presence of their former colonial rulers. The non- alignment policy was a direct outcome of that collective understanding and experience of political leaders and people across the Afro-Asian political spectrum. In addition to India’s long-standing tradition of peace and non-violence, the Gandhian influence, and a firm belief in peaceful co-existence with others in complete harmony, several key international conferences and meetings involving the thought leaders of the Afro-Asian world played a significant role in shaping the non-alignment policy of India and its many partners. India realised that it was neither necessary nor practical for it to join either of the power blocs. The Brussels conference In assessing the role conception of NAM by its constituent members, it is essential to evaluate the role played by the 1927 Brussels Conference. Convened in the Egmont Palace in Brussels in February 1927, the League against Imperialism and Colonial Oppression meeting was attended by 175 delegates representing countries across the world. More than 60% of participants were from countries under colonial rule. Jawaharlal Nehru (along with Virendranath Chattopadhyaya) participated in the conference as the 44 R. MISHRA
source: From non-alignment to multi-alignment assessing India s foreign policy shift.pdf

text: representative of the Indian National Congress. Other notable participants included Mohammad Hatta from Indonesia, Willi Münzenberg, Romain Rolland, Albert Einstein, and Henri Barbusse. The deliberations inspired the representatives from the colonised countries, including Nehru and other Asian leaders, to create a forum that would not side with the imperialist powers. That is why the Indonesian leader Sukarno later acknowledged the Brussels conference and the League against Imperialism and Colonial Oppression as ‘the start of an eventually victorious global liberation movement’ (Hatherley, 2021 ). Asian relations conference The Asian Relations Conference (ARC) is acknowledged as one of India’s most signifi - cant Pan-Asian initiatives which ‘constituted the first appearance of Asia in international politics’ (Mézard, 2006 , p. 20). The first ARC was held from 23 March to 2 April 1947. It was attended by 231 official invitees representing as many as 30 countries/entities/ institutions. Jawaharlal Nehru described the conference outcome as ‘an amazing success from every point of view’ and ‘a beginning of a new era in Asian history’ (Muni & Mishra, 2019 , p. 80). Highlighting the collective aspirations of participants in his inaugural speech, Nehru said (Asian Relations, 1948 , p. 2): It so happened that we in India convened this Conference, but the idea of such a conference arose simultaneously in many minds and in many countries of Asia. There was a widespread urge and awareness that the time had come for us, peoples of Asia, to meet together, to hold together and to advance together. It was not only a vague desire but a compulsion of events that forced all of us to think along these lines . . . because of this, the invitation we in India sent out, brought an answering echo and a magnificent response from every country of Asia. The conference helped firm up a common Pan-Asian identity of the newly independent countries of Asia. Together, these countries made some positive contributions to the United Nations including their support for the call for Indonesian independence. It also paved the way for greater cooperation between India and Indonesia and led to the convening of the Bandung Conference in 1955. Bandung conference While it is true that conceptually, the Brussels conference, the Asian Relations Conference, and India and the rest of Asia’s struggle for independence played their parts in shaping the nature and scope of the NAM, it was the Bandung conference that played a pivotal role in the launch of NAM. Termed by Sukarno as the ‘first interconti - nental conference of coloured peoples in the history of mankind’ (Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Indonesia, 1955 ), the conference was held on 18–24 April 1955 and witnessed 29 countries in attendance. Growing Asian solidarity was precisely the reason why the West felt uncomfortable about the Bandung Conference. The United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, and France did not like the idea of such a conference. Staying non-aligned in an intensely polarised world was an uphill task, especially when the US and the UK were trying their best to derail the Bandung meeting and its idea of a non-aligned, norm-based solidarity THE ROUND TABLE 45

text: among its members. The American and British attempts to sabotage the Bandung meet - ing naturally led to a general impression that the ‘USSR was perhaps more civil in its diplomacy.’ As Acharya ( 2017 , p. 78) opines: . . . The US along with Britain actively and openly sought to undermine by influencing the positions – even to the extent of providing anti-communist background papers and draft resolutions to its friends and allies . . . . It remains an important question whether NAM would have taken a different, less anti-American course had the administration treated the Asian neutrals with greater empathy and tactfulness and engaged them directly (rather than relying on Britain). Acharya rightly points out that the onus of shooing the ‘Asian neutrals’ lay with the US (and the Western bloc) and not the other side as some Indian foreign policy experts argue. Acharya ( 2017 , p. 79) states, Instead of seeking to manipulate the Bandung Conference through its proxies, the US might have shown more diplomatic tolerance for the event, which was by no means anti-Western talk fest and sought dialogue and understanding with the Asian neutrals that were the official sponsors of the meeting. A logical extension of this alternative might have been US support for the creation of a multilateral regional system led by India and Indonesia, involving Japan and Australia and with the eventual participation of the PRC. Instead, the US chose to base its East Asian security strategy on SEATO and its bilateral alliances (the hub-and-spoke system). The Asian Relations Conference started off on a strong note, and the Bandung con - ference continued the momentum. It not only disapproved of Western assumptions about Afro-Asian solidarity but also indicated that the non-western world had a normative agency in shaping the international order. Many of these issues are still reflected in ASEAN deliberations. Bandung challenged the ideational superiority notions of the West, which, as Acharya ( 2014 ) argues, contributed to shaping the ‘Western resistance to the political aspirations of the newly independent countries for equality and political autonomy’. Nehru’s role There is a general consensus that independent India’s foreign policy formulations, particularly the non-alignment policy, were deeply linked with the Indian freedom struggle experiences. It was shaped by India’s traditions of peace and nurtured by the Gandhian values of non-violence. Some even argue that since its inception, Indian National Congress resolutions on foreign policy issues were shaped by norms and principles that subsequently shaped Non-alignment (Prasad, 1983 ). As India’s first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru emerged as the architect of India’s foreign policy, particularly concerning India’s approach to the post-World War international order. Highlighting Nehru’s contribution, Damodaran argues (Damodaran, 1983 , p. 48): The idea of non-alignment from power blocs, as distinct from the earlier concept of neutrality or the later pejorative phrase ‘neutralism’ is associated both in its origin and in its evolution with Jawaharlal Nehru along with three or four leaders (Josip Broz Tito, Kwame Nkrumah, and Sukarno). 46 R. MISHRA

text: A newly independent India was mindful of the intricacies of the post-war world order. In his statements, Nehru also mentioned the possible role of ‘to be freed’ Asian countries. In his book, Discovery of India , Nehru states that the post-World War II international order would be dominated by the two superpowers – the US and USSR – and their bilateral dynamics would shape the international order. For him, however, a more prominent concern was the role and space for India’s Afro-Asian peers – a sentiment that resonated with Josip Broz Tito and Kwame Nkrumah as well. Highlighting these concerns (in the wake of a heightened US-USSR rivalry), Nehru writes (Nehru, 1946 , pp. 546–547): Where do the hundreds of millions of Asia and Africa come into this picture? They have become increasingly conscious of themselves and their destiny, and at the same time are also world conscious. Large numbers of them follow world events with interest. For them, inevitably, the test of each move or happening is this: Does it help towards our liberation? Does it end the domination of one country over another? Will it enable us to live freely the life of our choice in co-operation with others? Does it bring equality and equal opportunity for nations as well as groups within each nation? Does it hold forth the promise of an early liquidation of poverty and illiteracy and bring better living conditions? They are nationa - listic but this nationalism seeks no dominion over, or interference with, others. They welcome all attempts at world co-operation and the establishment of an international order, but they wonder and suspect if this may not be another device for continuing the old domination. Summing up Nehru’s conception of NAM, Acharya ( 2017 , p. 189) argues: Nehru’s concept of ‘non-involvement’ (which later fused into the broader doctrine of ‘non- alignment’) was practically an adaptive extension of the Western principle of non- intervention at a time when the two superpowers were violating the doctrine with impunity. The above statement highlights the concerns Nehru had about the emergent interna - tional order. He was keen to ensure that India and its peers got their due in the international system – that they become ‘rule makers’ and not mere ‘rule takers’. The Asian Relations Conference and the Bandung Conference amply demonstrated those aspirations. The raison d’être of NAM Faced with centuries of colonial exploitation at the hands of the Western Imperialist powers, it was natural for the newly independent non-western nations to keep their foreign and security policies independent, neutral, and away from any allegiance to either of the superpowers and their allies. Like India, many of these countries had to fight a long battle for their independence, which shaped their desire to play their due part in post- World War global politics. Some of the leading countries were ‘particularly keen to make contributions to the continuing struggle for peace and freedom. Such urges could find fulfilment only through the policy of non-alignment’ (Prasad, 1983 ). This preference to keep away from bloc politics was primarily driven by newly independent states’ desire to sustain the international pressure and survive and prosper domestically and internationally. Under the leadership of towering Afro-Asian states - men, many of these newly independent countries enthusiastically embraced NAM and its vision. Later, as the pitfalls of bloc politics surfaced, the normative role of the NAM THE ROUND TABLE 47

text: became more and more evident, but in the process, the Cold War power politics and politico-economic miseries of its members also undermined NAM’s normative role. In its original form, NAM was an astute diplomatic move that was mindful of India’s limited material capabilities. Post-partition India was economically weak and under tremendous pressure on the non-traditional security front. It had a vast population living in extreme poverty. The country was also facing a huge influx of refugees from across the border. For an economically weak and politically fragile India, it was logical to keep the focus away from a military-centric foreign policy. It was even deemed unne - cessary as Nehru (unrealistically) believed in good neighbourly relations with China while trying to balance good ties with both the USSR and the US. Under such a situation, barring international security challenges, maintaining a powerful armed force or keeping it prepared for any external/out-of-area operation was perhaps deemed unnecessary – an assessment which, of course, proved detrimental to India’s national security calculations vis-à-vis Pakistan and China. It is interesting to note that during those years, there was even a debate among the political elites as to whether India should keep the armed forces personnel strength intact or downsize it substantially, if not completely get rid of it. So, non-alignment was not just a principled ‘dream of neutrality but was rather based on a realistic assessment of India’s geopolitical situation’ (Pant & Super, 2015 , p. 749). Scholars argue that being a democratic country having close ties with the UK, India was a natural fit in the western bloc (Pant & Super, 2015 ). Theoretically, this assessment seems sound, but it would be problematic to imagine its acceptability in a newly independent country that had struggled against British imperialism for decades. Siding with the Western bloc would have been a political disaster in a country where ‘Angrezon, Bharat chhoro’ (Britishers, leave India) was a popular slogan, and where the revolution - ary armed fighters such as Subhas Chandra Bose were against the Western powers. To align with the Western bloc immediately after gaining independence would not have been morally right or practically feasible. India’s modest success in developing economic capabilities and failure to resolve its border disputes on time cost it dearly along the northern and north-western frontiers. The 1962 War dented India’s reputation in the Afro-Asian sphere while also compelling it to search urgently for reliable defence partners and suppliers. The China-Pakistan challenge along the border kept India ‘boxed-in’ militarily and strategically, leaving little scope for making any substantive normative contributions at the international level. In 1971, the then Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi signed a treaty of friendship with the USSR (while keeping the possibility for the same open for the US also; Rasgotra, 2016 ). As regards Nehru’s role in keeping Indian foreign policy non-aligned, he remained committed to the idea and followed it as far as possible. Several instances may be cited where, based on his idealistic assessment of the situation, instead of supporting the Soviet Bloc, he chose to side with the Western bloc. India’s unique positioning Unlike countries such as Malaya, which later gave birth to Malaysia and Singapore, and where the transfer of power was rather peaceful and negotiated among the political elites, India had to fight for more than a century to gain its independence which was also accompanied by a partition of the country along communal lines. For former British 48 R. MISHRA
source: From non-alignment to multi-alignment assessing India s foreign policy shift.pdf

text: colonies such as Malaysia, it was easier to remain aligned with the British as the common people were not against British rule (except some Malaysian Indians, who had to pay a heavy price for supporting Subhas Bose, the Indian National Army, and the Indian National Congress). Even after India gained independence and became a separate entity, Malaya remained a part of the British Empire. Even in Malaysia, where Tunku Abdul Rahman, a Britain-educated anti-communist political leader from the royal family, took the reins of independent Malaya, alignment with the West could not be sustained for long. Eventually, non-alignment became a guiding philosophy for Malaysian foreign policy after Tunku left office, and the ‘Young Turks’ took over Malaysia’s political scene. By the 1980s, Malaysia became one of the staunchest anti- Western (especially during Mahathir Mohamad’s Prime Ministership), non-aligned coun - tries in Asia. After the Tunku, the political leadership in Malaysia turned away from the West, with some even advocating that as an independent, sovereign, and self-respecting country, Malaysia should not align with the West (particularly the US). India did give the West, especially the United Kingdom, fair share of diplomatic engagement by joining the Commonwealth. Nehru also maintained cordial ties with the United Kingdom (and the West) often supporting their policies (e.g. the South Vietnam issue in 1950s). However, it would have been a political disaster to stick to the same Western powers which pushed the world into two World Wars and which were votaries of imperialism across the world. The polarised debates in Indian foreign policy discourse often point out this dilemma with neither side sufficiently explaining what could have been a better choice for India’s foreign policy in its early years. NAM and India: a critical appraisal One of the successes of NAM was that it not only helped in reaching a consensus on major political-strategic issues of global importance but, more importantly, it also drew countries closer in dealing with shared economic and developmental challenges. Kumar ( 1983 ) presents a three-fold perspective in assessing the contributions of NAM and argues that the level of ‘conformity between international goals and national interests in the NAM should be considered a measure of its strengths’. Furthermore, there has been ‘far greater conformity between international goals and national interests in eco - nomic matters than in the politico-security agenda’. This point is contestable, consider - ing that some countries secured economic favours at the cost of their politico-strategic autonomy in decision-making in certain instances. There is still a broad consensus that NAM did help some of the weakest member countries in coping with their major politico-economic challenges. Kumar’s third assess - ment that, in politico-security affairs, the members were more united on areas concern - ing either of the superpowers than themselves, worked as a double-edged sword. Over time, internal differences within NAM grew so much that they affected India’s own prime security interests – as will be discussed later. On the economic front, several developing countries, especially from the Afro-Asian region, economically benefitted from either or both the superpowers and returned favours in the form of tacit diplomatic suppport. For India too, the initial years of non-aligned policy brought home considerable economic gains for India, especially from the USSR, which brought in a substantial amount of funds and some projects. source: From non-alignment to multi-alignment assessing India s foreign policy shift.pdf

text: The China-Pakistan axis China-Pakistan relations have always been a major politico-military challenge, and a cause of strategic anxiety to India. For several decades, the China-Pakistan nexus was complemented by Pakistan-US ties. Undoubtedly, a newly independent India was under- prepared to deal with any major military aggression due to its lack of enough defence resources and military capabilities. In its belief that its neighbours would think alike on territorial boundary issues, the Indian leadership miscalculated Chinese intentions. China-Pakistan ties especially blossomed after the 1962 India-China war and subse - quently with Pakistan’s decision to unlawfully transfer 5180 sq. km territory to China in 1963. Nixon’s rapprochement with China in 1971 and the US support to Pakistan during the Bangladesh war of independence in 1971 turned counter-productive. All these aspects played a vital role in shaping India’s policy towards its north-western neighbours. Compared to the Cold War years, a remarkable shift has taken place in recent years. Among other things, the China-US trade war, their fast-growing strategic rivalry amidst China’s growing assertive postures, and the US-Pakistan rift have helped Indo-US ties grow in recent years. Indeed, India and the US are getting closer in strategic terms, but the relations are contingent upon the fast-changing dynamics of the Indo-Pacific and a range of other factors including India’s growing anxieties about a belligerent China. The rapid decline of the US-led liberal international order is also a major contributing factor. The US is reaching out to like-minded countries to ensure that the international strategic equilibrium is kept intact. Together, these factors have influenced Indian policymakers’ assessment of the situation on the ground vis-à-vis China. A realistic assessment of the situation has also helped India in realising the importance of engaging the US to deter China along the border. Having faced wars on two fronts, from China in 1962 and Pakistan in 1965, a still militarily weak India under Indira Gandhi inched closer to one of the two superpowers - the USSR. India and the USSR signed the Indo–Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship, and Co-operation in August 1971. While one cannot underestimate the importance of maintaining national security and territorial sovereignty, the decision did deliver a serious blow to the normative element of India’s non-alignment policy. JB Kriplani, a well-known political leader, warned about these pitfalls as early as in 1959 in his article published in Foreign Affairs (Kriplani, 1959 , p. 57): Neutral nations have to resist the temptation of inclining to one side or the other to gain temporary advantage. They must be impartial. They must avoid any action which may undermine the confidence of other nations in their neutrality and do everything that will strengthen it. Kriplani was a known, perhaps the most vocal, critic of Nehru’s China policy. In fact, he was the one who moved a parliamentary no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Nehru in 1963 – in the aftermath of India’s defeat at the hands of China in 1962. Explaining the delicate nature of India’s dependence on both the US and the USSR, M. K. Rasgotra explains (Rasgotra, 2016 , p. 405): In 1962, solid political and arms support for India came from the United States. A semblance of India’s non-aligned status was restored when the USSR also came in with generous military supplies on a sustained basis. But nine years later, to fight off the combined hostility of China and the USA towards India in the war for Bangladesh’s liberation, New Delhi had to enter into a virtual military alliance with the USSR. 50 R. MISHRA
source: From non-alignment to multi-alignment assessing India s foreign policy shift.pdf

text: Thus, albeit temporarily, a non-aligned India showed signs of multi-alignment even in the 1960s to ward-off the China threat. The multi-alignment in Indian foreign policy today is driven by a similar set of strategic concerns and necessities. Differences within NAM Over the years, especially during the 1980s, differences among NAM members widened, making it difficult for them to reach a consensus. Most of India’s efforts during those times were wasted without a consensus among NAM members (Rajan, 1982 ). Early signs of such rifts surfaced in 1955, not just between Nehru and Zhau Enlai – but also between India and SEATO (South East Asia Treaty Organisation). Differences between Nehru and Sukarno also widened before turning frosty in 1961 at the Belgrade conference. The 1962 India-China war, India-Pakistan war of 1965, the creation of the Malaysian federation and an independent Singapore, and, consequently, Indonesia’s Konfrontasi (con - frontation with Malaysia) in 1965 further damaged NAM. Assessing NAM’s performance, M. K. Rasgotra states (Rasgotra, 2016 , p. 405) that from Delhi’s perspective, despite the prestige and respect it commanded over the developing world, in India’s three crises moments – China’s invasion of India in 1962, India–Pakistan war of 1965, and during the 1971 Bangladesh war – NAM chose to stay non-aligned between India, China, and Pakistan. NAM members took the non-intervention norm a little too seriously to the extent of overexploiting the same. In several disputes among the members, the use of institutional mediation was not explored sufficiently to extract gains. A judicious use of good offices through a specialised agency was also not witnessed. From the late 1970s onwards, NAM became a victim of its internal bickering – with several countries from West Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia working at cross-purposes with one another. A further tilt towards the USSR also weakened the normative foundations of NAM. That said, NAM and its leading proponents did not have the luxury to think these issues through, as one could do in hindsight. Perhaps intending to answer these questions, scholars divide NAM’s Cold War history into two phases (Harshe, 1990 , p. 399). While politico-diplomatic dimensions dominated the first phase, starting right after India gained independence (and even before it; in 1944) and staying in existence till the early seventies, the second phase was marked by the predominance of economic and developmental issues. It lasted around two decades until the arrival of the post-Soviet unipolar world dominated by the US: India could not sustain the regional and global systemic pressures exerted on it. Consequently, the normative aspirations of India faded away as it failed to pay enough attention to its military and security capabilities. Sadly, for India, the systemic factors were far too powerful to ignore. India did not have many choices to deal with a security deadlock with China, which eventually ended with India’s loss in the 1962 war. In addition to exposing India’s security vulnerabilities, it also exposed the rifts within the Afro-Asian world, particularly India’s South and Southeast Asian neighbours. India realised that without strong military capabilities and some direct or indirect support from a superpower, it would not be able to safeguard and further its politico-strategic and economic interests. It was also after the 1962 war that several non-aligned countries sought overt or covert support from either of the two blocs and their respective leading powers – the US and the USSR.
