text: The Indian leadership also failed to take into account the domestic political develop - ments in China, particularly the emergence of the People’s Republic of China where aggressive nationalism and rectifying the so-called ‘historical mistakes’ were the key foundational pillars. Not paying enough attention to such critical details and perceiving China as just another post-Colonial state was a big mistake. India’s support to China was marked by a misplaced euphoria that clouded its ability to comprehensively assess the situation with its newly independent neighbour. Consequently, India failed to get a better sense of where Mao Zedong was coming from. History and popular culture are critical tools in making sense of a nation-state’s likely behaviour in a given situation. Unlike India, which gained independence through a non-violent peaceful struggle led by Mahatma Gandhi, the People’s Republic of China was built under the leadership of Mao. Perhaps, it was a mistake to believe that the two countries would approach foreign relations and boundary issues in the same manner. China was a wounded nation on whose face the scars of imperial exploitation and national humiliation were visible. Unlike India, it was deter - mined to correct history and was preparing for a complete unification by way of gaining territorial control over its ‘lost territories’ – Tibet and Taiwan. This lack of appreciation of Chinese history coupled with an fragmentary assessment of India’s national and territorial security challenges cost India heavily. India’s own historical experience in working with the British Indian government also shaped its boundary response to China. Norms over power To a great extent, a defining feature of India’s non-alignment policy was an unconven - tional approach driven by the desire to carve out its own space in a power politics-ridden bipolar international system (Harshe, 1990 ). True, India (and many of its peers) flip- flopped in that endeavour. However, considering the potential gains such an approach was worth the risk. Dulles’s rather bitter criticism of non-alignment as a ‘obsolete, ‘immoral’ and ‘short-sighted’ conception did not go down well with India (Patrick, 2012 ). Personal rapport between political leaders and policymakers has always been an important factor shaping relations – something which did play a role in turning India cold towards the US especially during the Nixon years. India’s own non-aligned policy was not the best fit in a world where countries were increasingly siding with either of the superpowers. For Pakistan, whose foreign policy was totally aimed at addressing the power disparity with India, it was essential to join either of the superpower blocs. With India having turned down the invitation to join a military pact, the US went ahead and signed military pacts with Pakistan, thereby further pushing India towards the other bloc. And yet, India did not sign any defence pact of any kind with the USSR until 1971. Even that decision was driven by the concerns raised by the US warning to India during Bangladesh’s war of independence. From non-alignment to multi-alignment The end of the Cold War, and the subsequent emergence of the ‘unipolar world’ led by the US, witnessed the rise of a hegemonic world order, which is now gradually giving way to a ‘multiplex world’ with its multiple theatres of competition and rivalries among regional and global powers. The relative decline of the US, rising China’s revisionist 52 R. MISHRA
source: From non-alignment to multi-alignment assessing India s foreign policy shift.pdf

text: tendencies, and emergence of the multiplex world order have made the US-India ties more important than ever. Since the 1990s, India and the US have been trying to get closer and build stronger partnerships. However, this relationship is not devoid of challenges. The US expects India to make clear choices in favour of the US-led coalition. It also expects India to cut off ties with Russia, Iran, and other so-called rogue states. For India, however, these are not just sovereign choices; these are based on hard-headed realistic assessments of the unfolding geopolitical scenario. To protect such decisions while bolstering cooperation with the US (and its allies), ‘strategic autonomy’ and ‘multi-alignment’ have been devised as India’s guiding principles. The decision to stick to Russian defence supplies is deeply embedded in India’s approach to having diversified sources of defence supplies, while Iran is one of the prime partners in the South West Asian region. With the rapidly unfolding situation in Afghanistan, Iran’s role for India has acquired greater salience. Indian policymakers are also careful not to give the impression that their policies are subservient to the US interests. The notion of strategic autonomy has not been pushed aside by Indian policymakers. Explaining India’s under - standing of strategic autonomy, the foreign secretary of India Harsh Vardhan Shringla ( 2020 ) in his address at the National Defence College in 2020 stated: The concept of “strategic autonomy” is a function of the prevalent structure of the interna - tional order making it a more relative concept as opposed to an absolute one. In today’s multipolar world, all countries are, at some point or the other, susceptible to external pressures . . . . As a result, the world around India changed fundamentally in the last few decades. It is also evident that the structural change that shaped the global order was predominantly a result of the shift in the economic balance of power. In addition, new and emerging issues threats from terrorism, cyber security, climate change, and pandemics called for India to adjust its policies to the new realities. Our strategic autonomy thus necessitated the association between an autonomous foreign policy and security decision- making capability and the preservation of material assets, both technical and economic. Shringla’s statement touches on the essence of India’s approach. A sovereign, independent, and rising non-western power cannot afford to remain oblivious to its strategic interests worldwide. India’s interests in Central Asia, the Persian Gulf, the Arab region, Latin America, Africa, Eurasia, and even in South Asia (Pakistan and Afghanistan) and Southeast Asia (Myanmar) may not necessarily be in sync with that of the US. Even with Vietnam, which has been lauded as one of the most promising US partners in the Indo-Pacific, India’s interests are not the same as those of the US. In Non Alignment 2.0 report, Khilnani et al. ( 2014 , p. 6) state: Strategic autonomy has been the defining value and continuous goal of India’s international policy ever since the inception of the Republic. Defined initially in the terminology of Non- Alignment, that value we believe continues to remain at the core of India’s global engage - ments even today, in a world that has changed drastically since the mid-20th century. Acolytes of the alliance system often tend to target India’s long-standing commitment to strategic autonomy as flawed and pretentious. Such assessments tend to overlook that for rising powers such as India, strategic autonomy functions as a tool to ensure survival and maximise leverage in any given situation To ward off such criticism and sufficiently explain India’s foreign policy approach, Dr. S. Jaishankar, the External Affairs Minister of India, officially pronounced India’s ‘multi-alignment’ policy. With strategic autonomy as one of THE ROUND TABLE 53

text: its tools, the multi-alignment policy aims to engage as many international stakeholders and partners as possible, based on India’s own politico-strategic and economic calculations. Highlighting the importance of multi-alignment in Indian foreign policy, Jaishankar states (Jaishankar, 2020 , p. 93): Taking off on non-alignment, it is sometimes useful to speak of multi-alignment. It appears more energetic and participative as compared to an earlier posture of abstention or non- involvement. He adds that multi-alignment facilitates a weaker player in soliciting or manipulating stronger forces to its own advantage (Jaishankar, 2020 , p. 62). Jaishankar’s reiteration of ‘multi-alignment’ in Indian foreign policy sums up the aspirations and strategic orienta - tions of a rising India. The critical importance of a deeper partnership with the US and its allies cannot be overstated. However, India is seemingly unwilling to compromise on its strategic autonomy in making foreign policy choices. This is witnessed in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, where despite the Western criticism and pressure, India has not gone against Russia citing its dependence on Moscow for defence equipment and regional strategic considerations invol - ving China. Partnership with countries such as Iran and Russia is pivotal to India’s presence in their respective areas of strategic influence. It is Russia, after all, with which India has opened a direct and dedicated channel of communication – a hotline between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi – to deal with the situation post-US withdrawal from Afghanistan. Likewise, India’s long-standing partnership with Iran would help India effectively deal with its strategic vulnerabilities emanating out of the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan. Both these issues are critical in shaping India’s relations with the US. Sensing India’s growing ties with the US, Russia has also normalised ties with Pakistan, compelling India to pursue ‘multi-alignment’ in its foreign policy, which may be seen as a pro-active, action-oriented, and more forthcoming version of the non-alignment policy. Highlighting the key facets of multi-alignment in India’s foreign policy, Jaishankar states (Jaishankar, 2020 , pp. 16–17): For the near term, India has little choice but to pursue a mix of multiple approaches, some orthodox and others more imaginative. But in all of them, partnerships with global interests could make a significant difference. Much of that would revolve around the West and Russia. But China, now the world’s second-largest economy, can hardly be disregarded in any calculation. Leveraging them all may not be easy but still no less necessary for that. Mastering mind games and playing hardball are also musts in a more visceral world. To do all that, it is vital that we come to terms with its complex dynamics. Only then can India successfully execute strategic policies for a new era. Clearly, despite India’s attempts to inch closer to the West, its pursuit of multi-alignment is likely to continue along with some time-tested elements of non-alignment. As S.D. Muni also noted in one of his social media comments (Muni, 2022 ): Dr Jaishankar’s statement that India cannot be a “pale imitation” of others defines Modi foreign policy’s (Modi’s multi-alignment policy) Nehruvian moment. This is what ‘non- alignment’ and ‘strategic autonomy’ were all about. Recent events such as the US withdrawal from Afghanistan, its withdrawal from multi - lateral economic frameworks such as the Trans Pacific Partnership (TPP), and policy flip- 54 R. MISHRA
source: From non-alignment to multi-alignment assessing India s foreign policy shift.pdf

text: flops on Indo-Pacific projects demonstrate that more than its commitment, the US policy endurance will be scrutinised by its friends in the region. Small, middle and rising powers of the Indo-Pacific region are still uncertain about the sincerity and endurance of the US commitment to the region on military, diplomatic, and economic fronts under all circum - stances. These security anxieties have motivated ASEAN countries to practise hedging in their foreign policies. A sustainable commitment of the US is a major factor shaping their national priorities and policies, and justifiably so. India’s multi-alignment policy cannot be appreciated without embedding it in the historical context and realities therein. Conclusion India’s non-alignment policy during the Cold War years was based on both idealism and pragmatism. Aligned with normative principles, it helped India steer clear of bloc politics. During the Cold War period, India not only had to focus on nation-building but also had several pressing issues to deal with such as the border conflicts with China and Pakistan, turbulence in the Indian subcontinent, and concerns related to nuclear weapons. Times have changed and non-alignment (in its original form) is no longer the mainstay of contemporary Indian foreign policy. Considering that the systemic realities of international relations have changed, it seems logical to shed some of the notions of non-alignment attached to the Cold War times as well. With regard to non-alignment - a major development that has taken place is India’s greater insistence on ‘strategic autonomy’, and the pursuit of multi-alignment underthe Modi 2.0 government. The ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, widening rift between Russia and the West, and the US-China tensions – all these develop - ments underline creeping polarisation, though with distinct differences, in contemporary global politics. India’s (and even Indonesia’s) claims to play a peace role in Ukraine war and now efforts to articulate the voice of the global south fall into the non-alignment mode although with several notable changes. Considering the fluid nature of international relations and great power dynamics, India is looking for a sufficiently wide strategic window – elbow room of sorts to manoeuvre effectively in regional and international scenarios. It is this insistence on multi-alignment that gives India the wiggle room to keep its defence ties intact with Russia and strategic cooperation with Iran functional while inching closer to the US and its Asian allies via the Quad. The sudden withdrawal of the US troops from Afghanistan and its willingness to engage China again is a sure sign of the unpredict - ability of international politics. India seems cognisant of these developments and has tried to keep its multi-alignment policy intact as the mainstay of foreign policy formulation. India’s insistence on multi-alignment policy also serves as a fine tribute to some of its cherished normative principles of non-alignment, even as multi-alignment has brought in stronger elements of hard-headed and pragmatic notions of foreign policy-making. text: India–China rivalry, border dispute, border standoffs, and crises Raj Verma School of International Relations and Public Affairs, Shanghai International Studies University, Shanghai, China Why did China intrude along the disputed border with India in May 2020? This question has baffled governments, policy makers, scholars, and analysts across the globe. There is no clarity even in the Indian government regarding China’s intrusions at multiple points along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in May 2020. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, Minister of External Affairs, India, stated that Beijing has provided five different reasons at different points in time for the incursions in May 2020. However, he did not elaborate on the reasons. 1 In June 2020, troops from both sides clashed in the Galwan Valley, leading to casualties on both sides. The last armed clash took place in 1975 when four Indian troops were killed in an ambush by Chinese forces at Tulung La in Arunachal Pradesh. The Galwan Valley clash has upended the bilateral rela - tionship, increased tensions, and frictions, and exacerbated the mistrust between the two “Asian giants.” 2 Multiple explanations have been provided by scholars and analysts for China’s incursions along the LAC in May 2020. These explanations encompass a broad spectrum including domestic problems in China, to domestic factors in India such as rapid pace of infrastructure buildup in the border areas by India, the abrogation of Article 370 and Amit Shah’s (Minister of Home Affairs, India) statement regarding restoration of Aksai Chin and Pakistan administered Kashmir into India, to systemic factors such as change in the balance of power which favors China vis-à-vis India due to rapid increase in China’s material capabilities in the new millennium, and India’s relations with other countries especially the burgeoning India–US ties. 3 This special issue examines the different explanations for Chinese intru - sions along the LAC. It provides a holistic explanation for China’s actions and also discusses various aspects of India’s and China’s foreign and security policies, India–China rivalry, domestic aspects of the two countries and their impact on the foreign policy and bilateral ties between the two countries, and the bilateral ties of the two countries with other countries and their impact on CONTACT Raj Verma rajneeshverma2000@gmail.com School of International Relations and Public Affairs, Shanghai International Studies University, 1550 Wenxiang Road, Songjiang District, Shanghai 201613, China INDIA REVIEW 2024, VOL. 23, NO. 5, 397–408 https://doi.org/10.1080/14736489.2024.2423996 © 2024 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC

text: the India–China ties and the border dispute. It seeks to inform policy and build a bridge between policy and practice. Before I proceed further, a word of caution is required. The article analyzes different plausible explanations for China’s incursions in May 2020. The contributors have been unable to establish causation or cause and effect relationship. This is due to the following reasons. First, as mentioned above, Beijing has not provided a proper explanation/ reason for its actions. Second, Chinese analysts have also not been able to offer a reasonable explanation. 4 Third, it has been extremely difficult for the contributors to get primary data especially access to Chinese government sources and information from Chinese analysts and scholars. Vast majority of the Chinese analysts/scholars contacted by the contributors did not respond to their queries for research. Those who did respond also provided no single reason/explanation to the contri - butors. In their responses, they all blamed New Delhi for the border problem without providing an objective and adequate explanation for their assertion. Thus, the contributors have employed a “mirroring policy” model/strategy. This strategy has been adopted in Chinese studies because it is difficult to conduct interviews with government officials and members of the armed forces in China. But by studying the views and analyses of Chinese foreign policy experts, one can gain insights into the factors that influence China’s foreign policy. The premise of the model/strategy is that the experts’ views mirror Beijing’s views to a certain degree. This is because the Chinese govern - ment can significantly influence the range of publishable views and research priorities of scholars/experts in China. Thus, when certain views on China’s foreign policy or China’s relations with other states appear in the debate, it implies they are acceptable to the Chinese government. 5 India–China rivalry India and China suffer from a positional, spatial, enduring, protracted, and strategic rivalry. 6 Positional rivalry is defined as competition between two or more states “over which state will benefit from possessing greater influence in a given global or regional locale.” 7 Positional rivalry between the two “Asian giants” is due to the competing visions of their country’s place in the interna - tional system and the pursuit of great power status in the Asia-Pacific and beyond. This quest is based on their historical national greatness: long and respected civilizational histories which they treasure and are proud of, and extensive empires that extended way beyond the present political boundaries. Both countries also have different views of history and the belief and determi - nation that their country will play a major role in world affairs. This has provided the edifice for the rivalry. 8 398 R. VERMA

text: The positional rivalry first emerged between colonial India and Republic of China (ROC) under Chiang Kai-shek, and later between the dominion of India (formed on August 15, 1947) and Republic of India (formed on January 26, 1950), and the ROC and the People’s Republic of China (PRC, formed on October 1, 1949). Elements of the positional rivalry were visible even before India became independent during the Asian Relations Conference held in New Delhi during April–March 1947. 9 India and China suffer from a spatial rivalry. Spatial rivalries between countries pertain to (disputed) territory, population, resources, location and may even be of symbolic significance. It emerges when two or more countries aspire to control some territory and continues as long as one country has an expectation – reasonable or unreasonable – to gain and maintain exclusive control over this territory. 10 India–China spatial rivalry is due to the dispute over Ladakh and Aksai Chin (including the Shaksgam Valley ceded by Pakistan to China in 1963) in the western sector, in the central sector across the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh (where the differences are minor and considered manageable) and over Arunachal Pradesh in the eastern sector along the disputed border. The territorial dispute is the legacy of British colonialism. Ganguly et al. argue that while the spatial India–China is impor - tant, the positional rivalry between the two countries is more significant in their overall rivalry. 11 Additionally, India and China suffer from an enduring rivalry because of persistent militarized conflicts between them 12 starting in 1959 and continu - ing in the twenty-first century including border clashes and standoffs in 1986, 2013, 2014, 2017, and other incidents, ambushes/skirmishes such as the killing of four Indian troops by Chinese forces in 1975 in Arunachal Pradesh, localized conflicts such as in Nathu La in 1967 and a border war in 1962. The rivalry is protracted because it has continued into the twenty-first century and there are little or no signs of abating in the near future. The rivalry is also strategic because elites in both countries have attributed an image of an “enemy” to the other country. While ROC and PRC leadership and elites considered India as imperial power and a rival after India became indepen - dent, India perceived China as a rival and an “expansionist” and “hegemonic” power after China’s annexation of Tibet in 1950–1951. 13 The India–China rivalry is also complex due to the involvement of regional and global powers such as the US, erstwhile Soviet Union, Russia, Pakistan, Japan, and other countries both in the twentieth century and in the new millennium. In the twenty-first century, to counter-balance a rising, aggres - sive, and assertive China, India has increasingly aligned itself with the US as Beijing tries to surpass Washington to become the pre-dominant global power. New Delhi has strengthened diplomatic, defense, and strategic ties with Japan, Vietnam, Australia, and other countries in East Asia, which are also wary of a rising China. Due to India’s increasing involvement in the Indo-Pacific, INDIA REVIEW 399

text: which is the epicenter of US–China rivalry/competition, New Delhi’s place in Beijing’s strategic calculus has evolved. Beijing’s perception of New Delhi is increasingly being influenced by how the latter responds to Washington’s Indo-Pacific strategy. Subsequently, China has further strengthened its strate - gic partnership with Pakistan. As China gets closer to Pakistan, India becomes closer to the US and Japan, enveloping the two countries in a vicious circle leading to increasing mistrust between India and China and deterioration in the bilateral relationship, with the two countries in state of persistent security dilemma which heightens the probability of escalation and conflict/war. 14 Intersection of India–China positional and spatial rivalry Scholars have argued that there is an intersection of positional and spatial dimensions in the India-China rivalry. Ganguly et al. contend that Tibet is not the epicenter of the India-China rivalry but it is deeply linked to the spatial and positional rivalries between the two “Asian giants” because the territories disputed between the two countries have historical links with Tibet. 15 India– China positional rivalry in Burma (now Myanmar) and the Himalayan states of Nepal, Sikkim, and Bhutan are/were linked to Tibet. Additionally, the 1962 India–China border war progressed as wars between positional rivals have proceeded in history with “multilateralization of the war” with India seeking aid from the US, the UK, and other Western powers. India’s defeat in the war had positional consequences as India was no longer considered a candidate for leadership in Asia. While China continued to play an important role in the wider strategic system in Asia, India, was confined to a position of a marginal player in Asia in the twentieth century and became more focused on South Asian affairs. India–China spatial rivalry continued after the 1962 war because the war did not resolve the border dispute. 16 Francine Frankel argues that the border dispute also raised the question of being the dominant power in Asia with both countries not willing to accept each other’s claim as acceptance would be perceived as deference to the other. 17 In 1962, India’s Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru stated, It is a little naïve to think that the trouble with China was essentially due to a dispute over some territories. It had deeper reasons. Two of the largest countries in Asia confronted each other over a vast border. They differed in many ways. And the test was whether any one of them would have a more dominating position than the other on the border and in Asia itself. 18 India–China border standoffs, clashes, conflicts, and war The Sino-Indian positional and spatial rivalry has led to numerous standoffs, clashes/ambushes/skirmishes, and conflicts along the disputed border in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. It also led to the 1962 border war in 400 R. VERMA

text: which India was defeated. This section discusses some of the major clashes/ conflicts/crises which have occurred along the disputed border culminating in the May 2020 incursions. In the late 1950s, there were multiple standoffs and skirmishes between Indian and Chinese troops along the disputed border. The first skirmish occurred in August 1959 at Longju, a few months after the Dalai Lama escaped from Tibet. Chinese forces initiated hostilities at Khinzemane and attacked the Indian post at Longju. After the attack, India did not return to Longju post, and the area has been occupied by China. The next skirmish was at Kongka Pass in Ladakh in October 1959 when ten members of an Indian paramilitary force were killed in an attack by Chinese forces. Seven soldiers were captured and the remaining escaped. The incident led to an uproar in India and heightened tensions between the two countries. Nehru realized the gravity of the border dispute and the two sides tried to resolve the border issue through diplomatic means. Border negotiations failed, and Nehru adopted the “Forward Policy” in November 1961 19 which has been provided as the justi - fication for the 1962 India–China war by some scholars. In 1962, China launched simultaneous attacks in the western and eastern sectors with underequipped Indian military crumbling under the Chinese offensive. The war altered the distribution of territory along the disputed border in China’s favor. While China restored status quo ante bellum and established the McMahon Line as the frontier in the eastern sector, its victory allowed it to capture and administer the Aksai Chin region in the western sector. The 1962 war sowed the seeds for antagonistic relations between the two countries and left deep scars in the minds of the Indian elite. 20 The next major conflict occurred in September 1967 at Nathu La and Cho La in Sikkim (which was deemed to be an Indian protectorate). A fence laying operation by Indian forces prompted an attack by the Chinese forces resulting in Indian casualties. Indian soldiers were better armed and equipped relative to 1962 and employed heavy artillery fire, and destroyed a large number of Chinese bunkers causing a large number of Chinese casualties. After a brief lull in fighting, Chinese forces tried to over run an Indian position at Cho La at the Sikkim-Tibet border. India had reinforced its troops in the region who repulsed the Chinese assault. 21 In 1986, a major crisis occurred at Sumdorong Chu in Tawang district in erstwhile North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA, presently Arunachal Pradesh). Chief of Army Staff, General Krishnaswami Sundarji launched “Operation Falcon” and airlifted a brigade to Zemithang, south of the McMahon Line and Indian troops occupied the heights in the Sumdorong Chu Valley after China occupied a seasonal observer post near Thag La ridge. From October 1986 to March 1987, India conducted operation “Exercise Chequerboard” to simulate India’s combat capabilities vis-à-vis China in the eastern sector. Tensions were exacerbated in February 1987 when India decided to change the status of INDIA REVIEW 401

text: NEFA to a full-fledged state of Arunachal Pradesh. The crisis brought the two countries to the brink of war. Diplomacy averted war with Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi visiting China in December 1988. The crisis was finally over in 1993, and border agreements were signed between the two countries in 1993 and 1996. 22 In the new millennium, the two countries signed border agreements in 2005, 2012, 2013, and 2017 to maintain peace and tranquility in the border areas. Despite the border agreements, border standoffs, and clashes between Indian and Chinese security forces have increased significantly especially since 2013. This can be attributed to multiple factors. Increase in economic growth in India has provided the resources to enhance infrastructure and improve connectivity on its side of the LAC (although India still considerably lags behind China regarding border infrastructure). This has allowed Indian troops to patrol in areas where they did not patrol before. The frequency of Indian and Chinese patrols has also increased due to better infrastructure. Both sides have also set up optronic equipment and surveillance devices to keep tabs on each other in certain parts of the disputed border. This has increased the incidence of Indian and Chinese troops facing off against each other. With increase in China’s material capabilities and President Xi Jinping coming to power in 2012, China has become more assertive regarding its territorial claims, and there is more aggressive patrolling by Chinese troops along the border. The nationalist Modi government in India has also espoused a policy of zero compromise on territorial sovereignty, and Indian security forces have also been patrolling more vigorously. There have also been reports of Chinese troops dismantling and/or destroying temporary embankments, construction materials, surveillance equipment, and rations on the Indian side of the LAC. Reports also indicate that China has continued to nibble Indian territory in the new millennium especially in Ladakh in the western sector. 23 Three major standoffs between Indian and Chinese troops occurred in 2013, 2014, and 2015. In April 2013, Chinese troops intruded 19 km into Indian territory in the Depsang Valley, 30 km south of Daulat Beg Oldi (DBO) in the disputed Aksai Chin region. The incident occurred 1 month before Premier Li Keqiang’s visit to India. Indian forces built an encampment 300 mm away from where the Chinese were camped. After 3 weeks of negotiations, both sides withdrew on May 5 with India agreeing not to build bunkers/sheds (this was an Indian riposte to the Chinese tent in Depsang) in the Chumar sector. In September 2014, during President Xi’s visit to India, Chinese troops intruded in the Demchok and Chumar sectors in Aksai Chin. This was in response to India’s construction of an old observation hut in Demchok in August 2014 which was dismantled as part of the 2013 agreement. Modi directly told Xi that border incursions and transgressions will adversely affect bilateral ties. New Delhi also contemplated special forces operation to evict Chinese troops who had intruded into the Indian perceived LAC. The 402 R. VERMA

However, Xi and China paid no heed to Modi’s repeated calls to delineate and demarcate the LAC. 24 Another small but significant altercation occurred in Burtse, east of DBO, in September 2015 in the Depsang plains. The crisis emerged after Indian security forces demolished a hut with cameras and solar panels (used for surveillance) built by China in territory claimed by India. As tensions mounted, both sides called for reinforcements. The standoff was resolved by local military commanders on the ground without intervention by the govern - ments of the two countries, which highlighted improvement in the bilateral relations. As a confidence-building measure, the two sides conducted a 12-day joint military exercise in China after the incident was resolved. China has been trying to change the status quo in the Burtse area to ensure that India is unable to overlook the Karakoram Highway, which links Pakistan-occupied-Kashmir with China, and to monitor the activities of Indian troops based in DBO airbase. 25 In June 2017, Indian and Chinese troops again clashed at Doklam, Sikkim, at the India–China–Bhutan tri-junction where Indian troops stopped Chinese troops from constructing a road in the territory disputed by Bhutan and China. India’s security concerns regarding the “Chicken’s neck,” a narrow stretch of land that connects mainland India with its north-eastern states, prompted India to stop Chinese road-building activity. The standoff lasted for 73 days. During the standoff, troops from the two countries were involved in a brawl in Pangong Tso Lake with injuries on both sides. According to some analysts, India and China were at the brink of war. 26 In May 2020, China violated the border agreements signed between the two countries with Chinese forces intruding at multiple points along the LAC and occupying a number of disputed positions – such as the northern bank of the Pangong Tso Lake, Galwan River Valley, Gogra – Hot Springs area in the Kugrang river valley, the Charding Nala area of Demchok and Y junction or bottleneck in Depsang Plains. They blocked/prevented Indian troops from accessing patrolling points on the Indian side of the LAC. India countered Chinese incursions in May 2020 which led to standoffs, fisticuffs, and brawls between Indian and Chinese troops in different areas along the LAC. On 15/ June 16, 2020, troops from the two slides clashed in the Galwan Valley leading to casualties on both sides. Both sides have blamed each other for the clash. text: strategic culture, domestic factors and politics in India, India’s infrastructure development along the LAC, China’s rising material capabilities and the shift in the overall balance of power between India and China, India’s foreign policy especially India–US relations, Sino-Indian relations, and Sino-Indian rivalry in the Indo-Pacific. In the first article, Prashant Kumar Singh debunks the belief/perception that “China’s ‘Strategy’ of Five Fingers of Tibet” is the rationale for China’s incur - sions in 2020 along the LAC. Some in the strategic community in India believe that President Xi Jinping is following the same revanchist policy propagated by Chairman Mao Zedong to attach Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan, Arunachal Pradesh, and Ladakh to China based on Tibet’s historical claim to these territories under the aegis of China’s historical tributary system. By examining the relevant historical literature and conducting interviews with experts on China’s foreign policy, the PLA, Tibet–China relations, and India–China relations, Singh highlights that the strategy of five fingers of Tibet is a “faulty prism.” Mao never postulated such a strategy and it was never practiced by China in its territorial claims/disputes with countries in South Asia. Employing this flawed lens does not augur well not only for Sino-Indian relations but also India’s relations with Nepal and Bhutan, because it leads to alarmist analyses. This is untenable for it will adversely affect public opinion and India’s foreign policy choices. In the next article, Rishika Chauhan argues that China’s 2020 incursions along the LAC are explained by China’s “salami slicing tactic” to grab territory controlled by India. Through this tactic, China makes small encroachments on the territory of another country and presents them with a fait accompli that is to either accept China’s land grab or go to war. These land grabs work slowly and effectively to alter the status quo and pose a major strategic challenge for the other country in the medium to long term. It allows China to undertake expansionism without recourse to war. Beijing has been employing this tactic for almost seven decades against India. It has also used this tactic against other countries with which it has sovereignty and territorial disputes including in the South China Sea. This tactic allows Beijing to achieve multiple goals including its core interests such as regime legitimacy and survival, economic growth and development, territorial integrity, aggrandize power and pursue regional hegemony. The salami slicing tactic led to incursions at multiple points along the LAC because Beijing knew from previous experience – in 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2017–that India will provide a robust response to its incursions. In the following article, Avinash Godbole argues that COVID-19 induced China to intrude along the LAC in 2020. He highlights that although China is powerful, its insecurity about its status makes it risk prone because it has a pessimistic security outlook. Beijing was under severe pressure due to international criticism for its mishandling of the COVID-19 outbreak. 404 R. VERMA

text: Beijing perceived the virulent criticism and vitriolic international environment as an attempt to contain China’s global rise. It also dented China’s status as a great power. The legitimacy of the Communist Party of China is linked to China’s status, and a benign international environment for China’s rise. In the past, Beijing has undertaken coercive military action when it perceived itself to be vulnerable and its strategic advantage was being mitigated or lost. Thus, China intruded along the LAC to showcase strength. It wanted to ensure that New Delhi did not perceive China as weak and not gain leverage over Beijing in the India–China bilateral relationship. It also wanted to send a message to other countries in the Indo-Pacific that COVID-19 will not prevent China from protecting its rise and status and overcoming challenges to its national security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. Raj Verma argues that two factors in conjunction explain China’s decision to intrude along the LAC in May 2020. First, the construction of border infrastructure especially the Darbuk-Shyok (DS)-DBO road which mitigates China’s military/tactical advantage along the LAC. Second, India’s Minister of Home Affairs Amit Shah’s statement regarding restoration of Aksai Chin and Pakistan occupied Kashmir (PoK) into India after the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019. Individually, these factors cannot explain Beijing’s deci - sion to intrude because the road has been under construction for more than a decade and India’s claims to Aksai Chin have not changed in the new millennium. Verma argues that Beijing considers that the border infrastruc - ture buildup by India especially the DS-DBO road would allow India to threaten Aksai Chin according to Shah’s statement. This is predicated on Beijing’s belief that India has become more risk prone, assertive, and aggres - sive in its territorial dispute with China under the Hindu nationalist Modi governments. Thus, anxieties and insecurities pertaining to Aksai Chin forced Chinese incursions in May 2020. Mahesh Shankar in his article draws on the rationalist theory to argue that China’s intrusions can be explained by the asymmetric material capabilities between China and India. Rationalist theories employ the difference in mate - rial power, both economic and military, between countries as the explanatory variable for state action especially in the context of war and peace. As a country’s material capabilities rise especially relative to its adversaries, its strategic calculus will change in the context of its most significant rivals. In the new millennium, China’s economy is circa five times India’s economy, and its defense expenditure is almost four times India’s military expenditure. China’s meteoric rise in the twenty-first century especially relative to India has pro - vided Beijing with more military options and opportunities along the disputed border. It has also led to a reduction in the intensity of internal and external threats faced by Beijing, which may have led to a conciliatory posture by Beijing in the past. The huge gulf in material capabilities between the two countries has led to a shift in the balance of power which has allowed Beijing to INDIA REVIEW 405

text: adopt a more belligerent posture in the territorial dispute with India. Beijing assumed that New Delhi will succumb to its aggression due to the gap in material capabilities between the two countries. Dalbir Ahlawat argues that China intruded along the LAC in May 2020 to teach India a lesson reminiscent of the 1962 war. India and China suffer from a positional and spatial rivalry in which the former supersedes the latter. As part of their positional rivalry, China attacked India in 1962 to reduce India’s influence in Asia and beyond, highlight India’s inability to lead Asia, enhance China’s international stature and portray China as the rightful leader of Asia. Beijing aspires to be the preeminent power in Asia and the most powerful country in the world by 2049. India’s status has increased significantly in the second decade of the new millennium due to high economic rates of growth and its strategic partnerships with the US, Japan, Australia, and other countries in the Indo-Pacific. Like in 1962, in 2020, China intruded along the border as part of its positional rivalry with India. It wanted to reduce India’s increasing clout in the region and force New Delhi to accept China as the preeminent power in the Indo-Pacific by checkmating their positional rivalry in the spatial domain. In their contribution, Harsh Pant and Vivek Mishra argue that India–US burgeoning ties in the new millennium especially after the Doklam standoff in 2017 both at the bilateral level and in multilateral settings may have provoked Beijing to intrude along the border in 2020. China’s rise, its quest to become the preeminent power in Asia and globally, and Beijing’s assertive and belli - gerent behavior in the Indo-Pacific especially along the disputed Sino-Indian border has provided the necessary glue for India and the US to strengthen their bilateral relationship. The expansion of India–US political, diplomatic, economic, defense, and strategic ties significantly affected the balance of power and security and stability in the Indo-Pacific. Beijing perceives strengthening India–US ties as an attempt to contain China’s rise in the Indo-Pacific and beyond. China intruded along the LAC to send a message to India not to strengthen its bilateral ties with the US and highlight the limits of Washington’s support for India in a conflict. The last two articles are prescriptive and prognostic in the context of India– China relations. The first article informs Indian policy makers by providing solutions to enhance India’s deterrence against China and prevent further land grab. The final article serves as the epilogue and examines the possibility of a conflict or a wider border war between the two “Asian giants.” The article by Sidharth Raimedhi focuses on how can India deter China. It highlights that in the new millennium, India’s deterrence vis- a-vis China has been eroding and is currently sub-optimal due to the asymmetry in material capabilities between the two countries. This is after India changed its deterrence against China from “deterrence by denial” to “deterrence by punishment.” The article advocates adoption of 406 R. VERMA

text: a generalized deterrence approach with a greater emphasis on denial. Deterrence by punishment is untenable post the Galwan Valley clash because of extensive military buildup by China including a large presence of Chinese troops close to the LAC. Moreover, India’s previous deterrence by denial strategy is outmoded. Raimedhi asserts that India can effectively deter China by significantly increasing military expenditure/power, estab - lishing a resilient domestic defense industrial base, reducing the focus on land warfare, and expanding the role of airpower instead of sea power to inject greater unpredictability. This needs to be buttressed by political and diplomatic measures including flexibility in India’s policy of strategic autonomy. The epilogue to the special issue examines the possibility of war between the two nuclear armed “Asian giants.” It highlights that the security situation along the LAC has deteriorated post-Galwan and is likely to further deteriorate in the future. This has ominous implications for regional and global security. Post-Galwan, the likelihood of both vertical and horizontal escalation between the two sides has increased tremendously, both along the disputed border and in the maritime domain (in the Indian Ocean), where India has a military advantage over China. Modi’s and Xi’s unwillingness to seriously discuss the border issue at the leaders’ level has compounded the security situation after the failure of several rounds of talks at the diplomatic and military level to resolve the border crisis. New Delhi’s refusal to publicly accept that China now forcibly occupies parts of territory administered by India has further compli - cated matters. This provides an incentive for Beijing to continue its attempts at land grab because these will be publicly denied by the Modi government. Third, the security dilemma has been exacerbated with both countries amas - sing troops and sophisticated advanced military platforms with both believing that holding and gaining territory is more significant than political dialogue. Finally, both sides have deployed new technologies and are employing brink - manship strategies which have elevated the dangers of further attempts at intruding or miscomprehensions which may lead to a conflict or broader war. INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW AMIT RANJAN Dr Amit Ranjan is attached to the Indian Council of World Affairs in New Delhi. 1 He holds a doctorate in South Asian Studies from the School of International Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, and has previously written for Asian Affairs. Email: amitranjan.jnu@gmail.com In May 2015, as the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi prepared to embark on a visit to China, foreign policy analysts began to speculate on what might be achieved by the visit. One of the most important ques- tions to be extensively discussed was what steps the two leaders might take to address the decades-old dispute over border demarcation between India and China. Questions over the India-China border are not a new phenomenon. They are asked whenever there is a Sino-Indian state visit. Despite having close to $100 billion of trade between them, China and India have failed to bring their frontier disputes to an end. In the 1980s and 1990s it was thought that the increasing economic cooperation between the two countries would act as a prompt to resolve their political disputes, but it has not. Military stand-offs and confrontations between border guards from India and China occur at regular intervals. To address their boundary disputes, they have engaged in frequent dialogues (17 rounds of focused dialogues can be counted between 1988 and 2015), but nothing substantive has yet been yielded through such engagements. The boundary disputes between India and China have their ultimate origin in the ‘Great Game ’ played during the British Empire. At present, the two main areas of dispute along the Himalayan frontier are the western sector (Aksai Chin around 37,250 sq km/14,380 square miles) and the eastern sector (Arunachal Pradesh, around 83,740 sq km/32,330 sq mile). 2 This article traces the roots of the boundary 3 dis- putes between India and China and attempts to discuss sources of tensions and probable solutions. 4 © 2016 The Royal Society for Asian Affairs Asian Affairs, 2016 Vol. XLVII, no. I, 101– 114, http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/03068374.2015.1129869

History The eastern sector and the McMahon line The eastern sector consists of three parts: the western part comprising the Tawang and Subansiri regions, and the central and eastern parts consist- ing of the Dihang and Lohit regions. 5 In this sector the genesis of the boundary dispute between India and China lies in the Simla Convention, which was held from October 1913 to July 1914 between British India, China and Tibet. 6 The Simla Convention was held in the aftermath of the collapse of the Qing Dynasty in China with the intention of settling the status of Tibet. British India had signed treaties with Qing China concerning the borders of Burma and Sikkim with Tibet in the late 19 th century.7 Before this period, the important trading town of Tawang was regarded as being under the control of Tibet. After Britain ’s brief intervention in Tibet following Francis Younghusband ’s 1904 expedition, Britain recog- nised Chinese claims to suzerainty over the territory in a 1906 agreement with China, and also in the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907. These agreements respectively provided that Britain would not annex Tibetan territory, and that neither Britain nor Russia would negotiate with Tibet directly, but only through China as an intermediary. However, after the collapse of the Qing Dynasty in 1912, the Dalai Lama regained power and declared Tibet independent, a move that was not recognised by the new Republic of China. In these circumstances, the Simla Convention was regarded as a necessity to resolve the situation: it was the hope of the British to secure their colonial interests in South Asia by maintaining Tibet as a buffer state between India and China. The Convention led to an Accord that Tibet would be divided into two regions: Inner Tibet, which would be under full Chinese control, and Outer Tibet, which is approximately coextensive with the current-day Tibet Autonomous Region of China. China agreed that the region would be under Chinese suzerainty but would never be converted into a province of China, and the British likewise agreed never to occupy it. On this basis, the Accord was initialled by the representatives of the three parties on 27 April 1914. However, two days after Chen I Fan, the Chinese representative, put his name to the document, the Chinese Government repudiated his signature. Their objections to the Simla Accord 8 were solely in regard to the 102 INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW

boundary between Inner Tibet and China and between Inner Tibet and Outer Tibet. However, apparently in the absence of Chen I Fan, the British representative Sir Henry McMahon made an agreement with Lhasa over the boundary between Outer Tibet and India. McMahon ’s proposal was to move the boundary line northwards from the foothills of the Assam Himalayas to its crest line, so that India would gain the town of Tawang and approximately 2,000 square miles of territory. The border proposal was accompanied by a bi-lateral trade agreement. However, in the absence of Chinese approval, this new boundary, which came to be known as the ‘McMahon Line ’, was not at that time endorsed by the Government of India or actively enforced on the ground. The position began to alter in the 1930s. The Government in New Delhi started to become concerned at China ’s increasing interest and presence in Tibet, and hence were inclined to become more hawkish on the matter of this particular frontier. When, in 1935, the British plant- hunter Kingdon Ward entered Tibet via Tawang without the permission of the authorities at Lhasa and was arrested, the McMahon line was revisited. Olaf Caroe, at that time a Deputy Secretary in the Indian Foreign and Political Department, researched the question of Tibetan authority in the region and virtually rediscovered the 1914 Simla Accord, which had to all intents and purposes been forgotten. Caroe held that the 1914 bi-lateral agreement between Britain and Tibet was valid and strongly advocated that it should be enforced. The text of the agreement, which up to then had been kept secret, was published. The McMahon line was indicated on the Survey of India maps, and in 1938 a small British patrol was sent to Tawang. This latter action brought a sharp protest from Lhasa. The Tibetan Cabinet, the Kashag, stated that Tawang and the surrounding territory had undoubtedly been Tibetan before 1914, and that acceptance of the McMahon line was contingent on British assistance in securing a de ﬁnite border between China and Tibet – an objective in which the 1914 Conference had failed. China maintained that any agreement reached between Britain and Tibet in 1914 was invalid without their approval. 9 The British did not attempt to repeat the 1938 patrol of Tawang. However, towards the end of the Second World War, the British, fearing that the Chinese would become more assertive in Tibet, attempted to enforce the McMahon Line more vigorously. The policy was inherited by India on independence. In 1954 the sovereign India recognised and adopted the McMahon line as the border between India and China. INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW 103

Although China formally contested this claim and sought a boundary demarcation along the lines of pre the 1914 accord, the Chinese position throughout the 1950s on the problem appeared ambiguous to Nehru. Following discussions with Zhou En-Lai in 1954, Nehru recorded the Chinese Premier had never heard of this [McMahon] line before though of course the then Chinese Government had dealt with this matter and not accepted the line … . Although he thought that this line, established by British imperialists, was not fair, nevertheless, because it was an accomplished fact and because of the friendly relations which existed between China and the countries concerned, namely, India and Burma, the Chinese government were of the opinion that they should give recognition to this McMahon line. 10 China was content to substantially accept the Eastern portion of the McMahon Line as the basis for the boundary demarcation between China and Burma (Myanmar) in 1960. 11 The western sector: the Johnson-Ardagh v Macartney-MacDonald lines India and China have had long-standing disputes over the Ladakh and Himalayan frontiers in north India. The boundary of Jammu and Kashmir with Xinjiang and Tibet is about 1,100 miles. Of this the frontier with Ladakh forms two-thirds. 12 The question of the Indo-China fron tier in this region originally fell to Britain 1846, when it added Jammu and Kashmir to its expanding territorial empire in South Asia. 13 Shortly before this, the Sikh Empire of the Punjab had annexed Ladakh to Jammu, and in 1841 had proceeded to invade Tibet. Following a con ﬂict with the Chinese forces in Tibet, who themselves staged a counter-attack on Leh and Ladakh, the Sikhs and Chinese made a peace treaty in 1842. Signed by the representa tives of Kashmir, the Dalai Lama and the Emperor of China, its terms included recognition of the tra- ditional frontiers of Ladakh and Tibet, and that neither side was to transgress or interfere with each other ’s territorial integrity. In 1847, following the British assump tion of the Punjab, the Chinese Government informed the British that as the boundary was “sufﬁ- ciently ” and distinctly ﬁxed, there was no need for additional measures for ﬁxing it. 14 Nonetheless, although parts of the border were clearly recognised, particularly the Karakoram Pass and the Pangong Lake, other areas, in particular in the remote and scar- cely-inhabited Aksai Chin, were not demarcated or otherwise deﬁned. 104 INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW

This lack of clarity was not to be resolved throughout the entire period of British rule. An early proposal in 1865 by William Johnson of the Trigo- nometrical Survey of India, following an unauthorised journey from Ladakh as far as Khotan, for a boundary which included Aksai Chin as part of India found no of ﬁcial favour from the British. A modi ﬁed version of this line, the ‘Johnson-Ardagh Line ’, which followed the Crest of the Kun Lun Mountains, proposed in 1897 by Sir John Ardagh, then Director of Military Intelligence, was also not accepted by the British at that point, in spite of arguments that it would be defen- sible against the danger of Russian expansion by way of that region. In 1896, following discussions between George Macartney, the British Consul-General at Kashgar, and local Chinese ofﬁcials, a further proposal for the frontier to follow the Karakoram Mountains and allowing China to take control of Aksai Chin was submitted to the British Government. This latter line was considered to be defensible against any threat from Russia and was accepted by the British. A note to this effect was sent to the Chinese Government in 1899 by the British Minister in China, Sir Claude MacDonald – earning the line the name ‘the Macartney-MacDo- nald Line ’. Macartney was informally noti ﬁed that there was no of ﬁcial objection to the British proposal, but no formal reply was received. 15 Despite this apparent resolution, there was no proper settlement. Follow- ing the collapse of the Qing Dynasty and the end of the First World War, the British advanced a claim on Aksai Chin up to the Johnson-Ardagh Line. In 1927, the British adjusted their claim back to a line based on the Karakoram Range. However, during the Second World War follow- ing a further perceived threat of Soviet penetration, the British claim returned to the Johnson-Ardagh Line. Nonetheless, up until the time of Indian Independence the British had made no attempts to establish a pres- ence in the remote Aksai Chin region. British and Chinese maps printed over the period showed a variety of boundaries amongst them, and the border remained without formal demarcation. India and Pakistan jointly inherited this problem from the British Empire, following the de facto division of Jammu and Kashmir between India and Pakistan after the ﬁrst Kashmir war in 1948. In 1963 Pakistan resolved its territorial disputes in the region with China, accepting the Macartney- MacDonald Line as the basis of the boundary (a settlement not recognised by India, which still claims the land thus ceded by Pakistan). However, the problems continued for India post-Independence. In 1954, the Johnson-Ardagh Line was claimed by India to be the boundary in the region, with Indian insistence that Aksai Chin was a long-standing part INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW 105

of Ladakh. However, during this period China, following its annexation of Tibet in 1951, constructed a road between Xinjiang and Western Tibet through Aksai Chin, whose existence was only discovered by the Indian Government in 1957. The Chinese position was that the Macartney-Mac- Donald Line was the only frontier which had been approved by agree- ment with the Chinese and that they were already in actual possession of Aksai Chin. There were tentative efforts throughout the 1950s to resolve the disputes diplomatically with Nehru ’s aspirations to create a Sino-Indian alliance, but towards the end of the decade a number of inci- dents in the border areas led to an increase in tension. The tensions were further inﬂamed by the Government of India ’s decision to give asylum to the Dalai Lama and others who ﬂed Tibet after the Chinese People ’s Lib- eration Army launched an operation to crush the 1959 Tibet Rebellion. In 1960 Zhou En-Lai unof ﬁcially offered to drop the claims in the eastern sector in return for India withdrawing claims over Aksai Chin, but Nehru refused to make any concessions or to negotiate until China withdrew troops from Aksai Chin. 16 Steps taken to resolve the boundary disputes After November 1961, to maintain its claim over these regions, India launched a more overtly confrontational ‘forward policy’, which involved establishing military positions north of the existing Chinese posts in the disputed territories in an attempt to cut off Chinese supply lines, and force a withdrawal. This was not only provocative but was based on an assumption that China would not retaliate. 17 At that time China was reeling under the disastrous impact of its Great Leap Forward programme of economic reform and facing threats of a military invasion from Taiwan and from US involvement in proxy con ﬂict through Laos. However, once the Chinese situation improved China attacked India in both eastern and western sectors on 20 October 1962. 18 The armed con ﬂict, which lasted for a month, resulted in Chinese penetration considerably south of the McMahon line in the eastern sector and up to the Macartney-McDonald line in the western sector. When China declared a unilateral cease ﬁre on 21 November 1962, they withdrew the People’ s Liberation Army forces to 20 km north behind the McMahon Line in the East, but continued in occupation of Aksai Chin, though again holding the PLA 20 km behind the Johnson-Ardagh Line. The ﬁrst attempt after the 1962 conﬂict to resolve the boundary dispute by way of mediation was made at Colombo. The Colombo Conference, an initiative taken by six non-aligned Afro-Asian countries – Ceylon (Sri 106 INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW

Lanka), Burma (Myanmar), Indonesia, Cambodia, the United Arab Republic and Ghana – to break the stalemate was held on 10 –12 Decem- ber 1962. It proposed, in the western sector, that a 20-km wide demili- tarised strip around the cease- ﬁre line in Ladakh “be administered by civilian posts of both sides ”, and in the eastern sector that the forces of India and China should separate their forces without the need for a speciﬁc demilitarised zone. China, however, objected to the establish- ment of civilian posts by India and unilaterally established seven posts of its own. 19 Negotiations on the basis of the Colombo Conference were dif ﬁcult, in that India interpreted the proposals as something to be accepted in their totality, whereas China understood them to be a basis for further discussion. India was also concerned that the acceptance of a withdrawal around the cease- ﬁre line – the ‘Line of Actual Control ’– would legitimise the Chinese presence in areas which had not practically been occupied by China before the 1962 War. After the 1962 War the ﬁrst high-level step towards establishing further negotiations to resolve the boundary issues was made by Nehru on 17 May 1964, when he stated that India would be prepared to negotiate with China if the Chinese Government agreed to remove their posts in Ladakh. This was contemptuously rejected by the Chinese Premier Zhou En-Lai and accusations were made that India was proposing these ‘array of obstacles ’ to make negotiations impossible. 20 Pandit Nehru, in a letter to Zhou En-Lai, also suggested various constructive steps including international arbitration that could resolve the boundary issue in peaceful way, but this was rejected by the Chinese government. 21 Post 1962, relations remained dif ﬁcult. There were regular skirmishes between border guards, one of which at Nathu La in September 1967 escalated to a ﬁve-day exchange of heavy artillery with the death of 62 Indian soldiers. China supported Pakistan in its 1965 war with India and built a second road across territory claimed by India, connecting Xinjiang with Pakistan. The 1963 boundary settlement between China and Pakistan (described above) which ceded territory to China claimed by India also weighed down relations. However, India ’s policy towards China took a major shift under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in 1975. She ordered India ’s special frontier force to draw back at least ten kilometres from their original position along the Indo-Chinese border and also dispatched an Indian ambassador to China in July 1976, thereby restoring the diplomatic relationship to the ambassadorial level some 15 years after it was downgraded in 1961. 22 INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW 107

When Mrs Gandhi made a return to power in 1980 the then Chinese foreign minister Huang Hua visited India in June 1981. At that time the two sides agreed to resume talks on the border issue at the level of vice-ministers, annually by rotation in their capital. 23 But still confronta- tion at the border was a regular affair, which increased in the middle of the 1980s with the substantive changes taking place in the international order.24 The Wangdong incident in the eastern sector in 1986, where Chinese troops entered territory claimed by India in the Sumdorong Chu Valley in Arunachal Pradesh and built helicopter landing facilities – an incident which brought the threat of another fully ﬂedged border war – prompted the then Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi to visit China and hold talks with the Chinese leadership on boundary issues. It is reported that during this visit to China in 1988, Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping had expressed his intention to leave the settlement of the territor- ial dispute to a “future generation”.25 Working in the spirit of addressing their border disputes the two countries agreed in 1988 to establish a Joint Working Group (JWG). As a follow-on to it, in 1993 they set up an expert group comprising diplomats, military of ﬁcials and cartographers for the purpose of subjecting to closer scrutiny each side ’s position and clariﬁca- tions on the Line of Actual Control (LAC).26 On the military front, in 1996 the two armies committed to limit the number ofﬁeld-army troops, border- defence forces, paramilitary forces and major categories of armaments along the LAC; to avoid holding large-scale military exercises near the LAC and to notify the other side of exercises involving one brigade (5,000 troops) or more; not to discharge ﬁrearms, cause biodegradation, use hazardous chemicals, set off explosions or hunt with ﬁrearms within two kilometres of the LAC; to hold regular meetings of border representa- tives; and to set up hot-line telecommunication links between local mili- tary headquarters along the LAC. 27 To assist the JWG, Special Representatives (SR) were appointed in 2003 after the then Indian Prime Minister Vajpayee visited China and stressed the importance of including political viewpoints in the solving of border disputes. Yet since 1988, despite these initiatives, more than a quarter of a century has passed but the dispute has not been satisfactorily resolved or managed. 28 To further de-escalate their tensions, in 2005 the two countries signed a treaty setting out guiding principles to manage incidents at the border as well both sides’ aspirations for a ﬁnal peaceful settlement of all bound- ary disputes. Again, in 2013 India and China signed a border defence cooperation agreement to ensure that border patrols could not trigger an exchange of ﬁre between the border guards of the two sides. 108 INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW

Unfortunately, the disputes remain. During his visit to China in 2015, the Indian Prime Minister maintained “On the boundary question, we agreed that we continue to explore a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable res- olution. We both reiterated our strong commitment to make all efforts to maintain peace and tranquility in the border region ”. 29 Even after these more recent steps to defuse tensions, they still occur but have not escalated above an ‘accepted’ level. In 2013, Chinese Premier Li Keqiang’s (19 –22 May) visit to India was preceded by a Chinese intru- sion in Ladakh near the Daulat Beg Oldie. China withdrew only after India agreed to demolish its bunker in Chumar, a concession which China had been seeking for several months. The joint statement between the leaders on the occasion of the visit did not touch the intrusion issue. 30 A similar incident was repeated in the western sector in 2014, fol- lowing the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Chinese government continues to consider certain parts of the eastern and western sectors as its own sovereign territory. Any sugges- tion to the contrary is met with a str ong reaction by the Government of China and Chinese media. For example, on 17 January 2015, replying to a question after delivering the Sapru House Lecture on “Special Partnership for the Era of the Indo-Paci ﬁc” at the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA), the Japanese Foreign Minister Fumio Kishida mentioned the status of Arunachal Pradesh (China calls it North East Frontier Agency). There was an outcry amongst the Chinese media, and a protest was lodged by the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The impact was such that Kishida had to defend himself. He told the reporters in Brussels on 19 January that “India basically and effectively controls [ the region], and China and India are continuing consultations on the border issue. I made the remark taking these facts into account ”. 31 Solution and stymie As the root of problem lies in the past, the solution can be found only after re-visiting the history. Inc remental changes or agreements can only resolve the immediate issues, which still leave a lot of space for military confrontation between the t wo countries. Re-visiting the past to resolve the issue demands compromise, adjustments and political determination. This is possible only when there is a consensus to do so among the political leadership, institutions and dominant political INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW 109

constituencies. This is undoubtedly a dif ﬁcult exercise on account of bitter memories of history, as well as existing socio-political narratives about each other in the respective countries. A move to address the bit- terness requires a re-negotiation with history and review of the past to sketch out a draft for the future. Unless this frank reassessment happens the likelihood of settling the India-China boundary issues through a series of incremental measures, as has taken place over the last quarter century, is bleak. China is certainly capable of compromise. Taylor Fravel maintains Beijing has often been very ﬂexible about principles in reaching territorial settle- ments with other states. The decisive factor is the judgment of China ’s leaders about what best serves their national interests – ﬂexibility or in ﬂexibility on prin- ciple. In relation to India, rather than being ﬂexible Beijing has chosen to stand on inﬂexible principle, making a solution of the territorial con ﬂict less likely. 32 As an example, following the disintegration of the Soviet Union China took the ﬁrst step with the newly emerging Central Asian Republics to settle its border disputes with them. In a few of these cases, it even made signi ﬁcant adjustments to compromise on its pre-1990 territorial demands. As regards India, in previous years India indicated that a solution on the lines of an ‘LAC plus’ might be acceptable, which would consist of the status quo remaining in the eastern sector accompanied by Chinese concessions in the western sector. Further discussions after 1985, again taken up in 2005, looked at a compromise where China hinted at making concessions over Aksai Chin but only in return for signiﬁcant con- cessions in the eastern sector; it should be noted that given the ever increas- ing developments in transport infrastructure and connections to Tibet, the strategic importance of Aksai Chin to China is not as great as it was in the past. Nevertheless, no mutually agreeable solution has yet been found. 33 In 2015, during her visit to China, India ’s External Affairs Minister, Mrs Sushma Swaraj, had talked about the need for ‘out-of-the-box’ solutions to resolve long-pending territorial disputes between India and China. 34 These ‘out-of-the-box’ solutions may be similar to those mentioned above to resolve boundary disputes between the two countries. India’s and China ’s divergent national interests remain a major hurdle in resolving their boundary disputes, prompting them to maintain a confron- tational posture. Both of them are parallel rising powers, who are (wrongly) perceived to be bound to collide over time. Their confrontation is further escalated by continuing interactions with each other ’s arch- 110 INDIA-CHINA BOUNDARY DISPUTES: AN OVERVIEW

rivals. China maintains a close relationship with Pakistan, and is sus- pected (sometimes correctly) by the Indian establishment of supporting it even at the cost of India's security interests. In 2015 China gave support at the United Nations to Pakistan over the matter of Zaikur Rehman Lakhvi, a ringleader of the 2008 attacks on Mumbai. Coming immediately after the visit by the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to China in 2015, this caused a signi ﬁcant souring in the relationship of India and China. Likewise India's engagement with the USA and Japan has caused discontent in Beijing. In January 2015, whilst the US Presi- dent Barak Obama was in India, a carefully worded article appeared in the Global Times and People’s Daily, the of ﬁcial newspapers of the Chinese Communist Party, cautioning India not to fall into the “trap” being laid to pit New Delhi against Beijing by Washington as part of its “pivot to Asia ” doctrine, but voicing an offer by Xi Jinping to lift China’s strategic partnership with India to a “higher level” in recompense for such carefulness. 35 As a checkmate, during Obama ’s visit to India, Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff General Raheel Sharif embarked on an ofﬁcial visit to China. The Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi, in his meeting with General Raheel Sharif, stated that Pakistan was China ’s irreplaceable all-weather friend and that both countries were part of a shared destiny. 36 Conclusion The two sides could resolve their international boundary problems by simply accepting the areas and regions which are at present under their control. This seems to be an easy solution, but in reality it is not. The two countries have to declare that they are accepting their present situ- ation and ultimately have to avoid confrontation on lines drawn in the past. But in taking such a path, they may not be supported by their respective domestic constituencies, political institutions and international actors. Hence, the ‘out-of-the-box’ solution still awaits discovery. NOTES 1. The views expressed are those of the author and do not re ﬂect those of the Indian Council of World Affairs. 2. 3. In this article a clear distinction is drawn between the words ‘boundary’, ‘border’ and ‘frontier’, which are not synonyms. A boundary line has to be very accurately depicted, with precise coordinates and marked by well-known geographical fea- tures. For it to be an effective instrument, it must not only be properly delineated on a map but also visible and effectively demarcated on the ground. This can be cate- gorised into: natural boundaries, astronomical or mathematical boundaries and his- torical boundaries. ‘Border’ refers to zones of indeterminate width that form the outermost parts of a state that are bounded on one side by a national boundary. ‘Frontier’ is a vague and indeﬁ nite term. It has two conceptual meanings. The ﬁrst concept means a political frontier that divides two states, and it need not be under the control of either state. The second concept of a frontier de ﬁnes it with reference to ‘settlements’ within a single country. It represents the distinction between occupied and controlled land. Many countries prefer to use ‘frontier zones’ rather than boundary lines because it absolves them from negotiating and policing speci ﬁc boundary lines that may entail a heavy ﬁnancial expenditure. text: [ 21 ] roundtable • regional perspectives on u.s. strategic rebalancing India: Between “Strategic Autonomy” and “Geopolitical Opportunity” C. Raja Mohan T he U.S. rebalancing strategy toward Asia announced by the Obama administration has been long overdue. Despite the end of the Cold War in Europe, policy inertia in Washington meant that a large portion of U.S. military resources continued to be deployed in the Atlantic. This imbalance was further exacerbated by the two prolonged and costly military deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. A new consensus also prevailed in Washington that there was no potential great-power peer competitor to the United States and that it thus had the luxury of experimenting with nation-building and democracy-promotion in the Middle East and beyond. The costly interventions in Iraq and Afghanistan have disabused many in the U.S. foreign policy establishment of their post–Cold War beliefs about the efficacy of American power in changing the world for good. They have instead been persuaded that it is time for the United States to look after its own vital national interests. Moreover, the U.S. diplomatic and military pivot to Asia had been delayed by a misreading of China’s intentions toward the United States over the years. Many in the United States were quite convinced that the rise of China was likely to be peaceful and that China could, with some purposeful U.S. effort, be integrated into the current international system. This assumption, however, became untenable after President Obama’s unsuccessful visit to China in November 2009. Beijing, which seemed to have concluded that the United States was on an irreversible path of decline, had no interest in Washington’s strategic reassurance or its offers to jointly manage the problems of the world. Worse still, China’s military and political assertiveness during 2009–11 demanded urgent responses from the Obama administration. Any further delay in announcing the pivot would have weakened U.S. alliances in Asia and raised the threat of China’s successful “Finlandization” of the continent’s rimland.
